I understand that some members of the Committee desire to speak generally on the question, and while an opportunity Is , being afforded them, I

shall endeavour to see if we can get the regulations in the form suggested by the hon. member.
Mr. CR'ONYN: Mr. Chairman, if I am now in order, I desire to make a few remarks on this clause and to suggest two amendments thereto. In the first place, when the resolution on which this Bill is founded came up for discussion, I suggested an amendment which was not approved by the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White), and which was dropped. Upon reading his remarks in Hansard, I take it that the basis upon which the Government is acting in this matter is set out in these words by the Acting Prime Minister on page 2440 of Hansard:
The principle which should underlie the action of the Dominion with respect to legislation of this kind in recognition of the rights of the provinces to enact such legislation within their jurisdiction as they may deem proper.
And again, on page 2438, the Acting Prime Minister states:
I should be prepared to consider an amendment to the resolution which would provide for the importation into a province of wine not exceeding the alcoholic standard authorized hy the law of that province. Such an amend- [DOT] ment might provide for importation from a country outside of Canada, or for transportation from another province in Canada, into any province where such a law as I have mentioned is in effect.
Following the reason of the Acting Prime Minister, I feel it will be necessary to drop my former suggestion. I note that his position, which is also that of the Cabinet, has been approved by a body called, I think, the Dominion Alliance, which is prepared to endorse the Government in accepting the provincial view on matters concerning prohibition. I, therefore, do not purpose making any general remarks on the Bill itself. It would be futile to mention the fact, and I understand it to be a fact, that a petition of 1,500 Trades Unions was presented to the Government last February asking for an increase in the strength of beer. The answer, in View of the attitude of the Government, would be logically this: You must go to your provincial legislature and request it to increase the strength of the beer, if that is your desire. It would be useless to discuss the fact that in various states of the Union and in a number of European countries, beers of a strength of from two to three per cent alcohol by weight are declared to be non-intoxicants and are advocated very strongly by temperance societies and other bodies in those countries. But I do question whether this new Bill follows the provincial law, and I hope to be able to submit to the Committee a statement, which, if the Committee reach the opinion which I have reached, may cause them to favour the amendments which I shall suggest.
I want to take the case of Ontario as an example. I have no familiarity with the laws of the other provinces, but I have before me a copy of the Ontario Temperance Act. It is necessary for the consideration of this subject that the Committee follow as closely as they may be able, the law of Ontario as, in my opinion, it stands to-day. Under section 40 of the Ontario Temperance Act passed in 1916, there is a sweeping clause prohibiting any person from selling any liquor,-which, under the interpretation clause, is defined to be any liquid having an alcoholic strength of more than 2J per cent proof spirits. Section 41 is another sweeping clause and it provides, that no person by himself, his clerk, servant or agent shall have or keep or give liquor in any place wheresoever, other than in the private dwelling house in which he resides, without having first obtained a license under this Act authorizing him so to do. Then there follow three clauses to which I wish to draw the attention of the Committee, and which may be classed as clauses of exception. I do not desire to read all of each of these clauses as portions do not affect the question at issue, but I hope to read all the words which have any bearing on the subject. Section 43 provides, amongst other things-and this section was enacted first in 1916, and amended in 1917:-
Nothing in section 41 contained si,ad prevent common carriers or other persons from carrying or conveying liquor from a place outside of Ontario to a place where the same may be lawfully received and lawfully kept in Ontario, or from a place where such liquor is lawfully kept and lawfully delivered within Ontario to a place outside Ontario, or from a place where such liquor may be lawfully kept and lawfully delivered in Ontario to another place in Ontario where the same may be lawfully kept, or through Ontario from a place outside of it to another place outside of it.
That clause, as will be seen, deals with common carriers or other persons interested in transportation. Then section 45 reads:
Nothing herein contained shall prevent any brewer, distiller or other person duly licensed by the Government of Canada, for the manufacture of spirituous, fermented or other liquors, from keeping or having liquor manufactured by him in any building wherein such manufacture is carried on, provided such building does not contravene the provisions of section 39 hereof, or for selling liquor therefrom to a person in another province or in a foreign country-*

I just want to emphasize that line, which is repeated in the next section.
-or for selling liquor therefrom to a person in another province or in a foreign country or to a licensee under this Act, or to the keeper of a liquor warehouse within the meaning of section 46.
Then this clause was amended at the last session of the legislature by repealing certain words and adding these:-
Nor shall it prevent a distiller selling alcohol to a wholesale druggist.
Then subsection (1) of section 46, which is very much along the same line as the fast section I have read, reads:-
Nothing herein contained shall prevent any person from having liquor for export sale in his liquor warehouse, provided such liquor warehouse and the business carried on therein complies with the requirements in subsection 2 hereof mentioned, or from selling such liquor from such warehouse to persons in other provinces or In foreign countries.
Under these sections of the Act-and 1 do not think there are, in that very voluminous Act, others which materially affect the provisions of those sections-the law of Ontario is clear that while one could not sell liquor having a strength of more than 2J per cent proof spirits in Ontario, it was possible to manufacture and export to places outside of Ontario liquor of a greater strength. Since that Act was passed, the Orders in Council, of which those now before us are a consolidation, came into effect, and in 1918 the Legislature of Ontario added section 154 to the Ontario Temperance Act, which reads:-
During the time any statute of the Parliament of Canada or any Order In Council passed thereunder is in force, the effect of which is to prohibit the transportation of liquor into or out of this province for any purpose, sections 43, 45, 46 and section 139 of the Ontario Temperance Act shall be deemed to be suspended to the extent necessary to conform to the provisions of such statute or order.
I would call the attention of the Committee particularly to the words "shall be deemed to be suspended." I submit that the real effect of the Bill before the Committee is not to implement the provincial law, but actually to supplant it. The pro-, vincial law, as I hope I have made clear, did allow the export of liquor of a greater strength than that mentioned, and the Order in Council actually prevents it. It is quite true it may be argued that the Ontario Legislature suspended the operation of the four sections I have mentioned during the continuance of the Orders in Council, but if we now confirm by this legislation those Orders in Council, are we
]Mr. Cronyn. [
not virtually legislating for Ontario? That is the effect, and if I cannot make that clear, I must confess to failure.
It may be argued that Ontario recognized the Orders in Council and was only too glad to lay the burden upon the shoulders of the Dominion-words to that effect were used in a former discussion. I rather take it that Ontario desired no clash of jurisdiction between the province and the Dominion and was quite willing to supplement the Dominion Order in Council by saying "While that Order in Council is in force we shall suspend the effect of our Act."
In order that the Committee may understand the effect of the amendment I shall propose, I will read subsection 1 of section 3 of the regulations, appearing on page 4 of the Bill, as amended by section 1 of the Bill:
No person shall make or manufacture intoxicating liquor or cause intoxicating liquor to be made or manufactured within the Dominion of Canada after the first day of April, one thousand nine hundred and eighteen: Provided that in case the sale of intoxicating liquor of any class for beverage purposes is permitted in any province, this regulation shall not apply to the manufacture of such intoxicating liquor in such province.
Section 1 of the Bill strikes out all the words after "province" in subsection (1) of section 3, so that the subsection as amended will read as above. Now my amendment is that the last three words "in such province" shall be struck out. The proviso will then read as follows:
Provided that in case the sale of intoxicating liquor of any class for beverage purposes is permitted in any province, this regulation shall not apply to the manufacture of such intoxicating liquor.
In other words, as the law of Quebec allows beer of a strength of 2.96 per cent to be manufactured and sold in that province, the other provinces may lawfully manufacture beer of that strength.

It would be just as unlawful for a brewer to sell beer of that strength in Ontario as to sell to the public the stronger beer which the brewers now manufacture and sell for medicinal purposes to licensed vendors.
Combined with the amendment I have proposed, I also suggest an amendment to subsection (3) of section 3 of the regulations, and in this case my amendment has to be

read into the amendment proposed by the Government, I will now read subsection 3 as it will read with the combined amendment:

I leave out the proviso which then follows, because it has only a temporary effect and does not govern this case at all, and I will read the second proviso with the combined amendment:
Provided that this regulation shall not apply to the sending, taking, transporting or delivering any intoxicating liquor lawfully manufactured in any province to any place where such intoxicating liquor may lawfully he sold.
Hon. members will see that my amendment strikes out the words "in such province" from the amendment appearing in paragraph (d) of section 1 of the Bill. I quite agree with the hon. member (Mr. Bureau) that it is most difficult to follow the Bill in its present form. (The net effect of the two amendments I have proposed is to allow the manufacture of beer of the strength permitted by the province of Quebec in any province of the Dominion, It does not permit the manufacture of any other liquor; it would, of course, permit the manufacture of wine up to the Quebec strength, but that is already provided for under a special proviso. It would also permit the export of that beer not only to the province of Quebec but to any foreign country where it can lawfully be sold. That is the total net effect of striking out the words " in such province" in the two subsections.
It restores to the. breweries throughout Canada-because it affects only the breweries, as I read the Act-their right to export ale of only Quebec strength to any country where it may lawfully be sold.

That is the proposition as embodied in the amendment I have suggested. Under the Bill as brought down here, while you can import into Quebec wines of Quebec strength from anywhere in the world including Ontario, you cannot export from Ontario or any province beers of any strength greater than 2J per cent proof spirit. That is the rule in Ontario, and, I understand, it is the same rule throughout the rest of Capada. The curious fact should be noted that if Ontario is so ill advised as to follow the example
set by Quebec-some people may quarrel with my phraseology describing it as ill advised^-and allow beer and wine of limited strength to be sold there, while Ontario could manufacture that beer it could not under this Act be sold outside of Ontario; and Quebec could not export her beer into Ontario, nor could any other province. As I said, I did not come prepared to discuss the general question, but I do not want this Committee to be under any misapprehension as to my view thereon. I am delighted to testify to the benefits derived from the abolition of the sale of ardent spirits under the Ontario Temperance Act, and I would be very sorry to see that Act repealed. But I am also of the opinion that the best measure of temperance to-day is that one, or something akin to it, adopted by the province of Quebec. I therefore move:

Mr. .THOMAS FOSTER:	The question
is, do we or do we not want a " dry " Canada? The answer is; we do. Considerable effort has been made to prove that the working men are anxious to return to the old condition of things. Even Gompers has given his view on liquor drinking and is rather encouraging the use of strong drinks among working men. From my experience I will venture to say, notwithstanding the endeavours that are made to draw the workman into this issue, that the liquor interests are involved in the attempt to revert to the old condition of things; and before I conclude my remarks II think I shall be able to convince the Committee that the workingmen generally do not want that condition. It is untrue that the workingmen are asking for it. But there are certain interests that are making capital out of the question for their personal advantage and at the expense of the workingmen. Let tis consider the question; from eome concrete standpoints. Do the railway companies, for instance, want to employ men who indulge in drinking either wine or beer? My experience is that any man who shows any indication of being addicted to the drink habit is turned down, and there is no use whatever for men of his type. Then take the manufacturers- and we have many of them in this Chamber. One such gentleman is sitting very close to me and no doubt he employs hundreds of men. I would like to ask him if he or any other manufacturer would employ to operate machinery men who showed signs of intoxication. I think not. And take the banks. I know of one instance in which a bank was wrecked through over-indulgence on the part of one of its principal men; and in another case of which I am aware, a man who had imbibed too freely lost one of the best positions in connection with the management of a bank. And in connection with the steam ship companies no man who is addicted to the drink habit even in the slightest degree will be employed, for we know that accidents have frequently happened and lives have been lost because men employed in occupations of this kind have given way to drink. I remember a few years ago that to be a school trustee or an alderman or a controller, a mayor or-member of Parliament, one could not succeed unless he had been

[DOT] and I might mention a rather amusing incident. I know of a candidate who catered extensively to people of this type. He would call into the saloon perhaps about twenty or thirty men, and there would be in all some hundred men in the saloon. He would purchase drinks for all the "boys" who, as soon as they had quaffed their fill, made their escape. The candidate could not understand it, but when he got to tRe next corner the men were all there as dry as ever. He went the rounds for a couple of hours, and the crowd grew larger and larger at each saloon, until after a while there was no saloon large enough to accommodate the men who had been trying without success for hours to slake their thirst. That condition of things has passed away, and we do not want a return to it. We know the debauching effect drink has had on the people generally, even when supplied by candidates who wanted to ensure their elections and to be considered pretty good fellows into the bargain. In satisfying those . who were ready to drink, they were only injuring men who would be better off without liquor. I wish to call the attention of the House to two or three statements which I shall quote as bearing upon this important question:
Prohibition Extending in Europe.
The trend of public opinion throughout Europe is ail against the Liquor traffic. Legislation prohibiting certain classes of spirits had been adopted prior to the war, and, since the outbreak of hostilities this has been largely extended, both in belligerent and neutral ooun- , tries, while beer and wine have been prohibited in some countries and greatly restricted in others.
Total prohibition has been enacted in Russia, Roumania, Finland, Iceland, Greenland, the Faroe Island, and among the North Sea Fisheries. Absinthe and similar spirits have been prohibited in France, absinthe in Switzerland,

speechtext:
Italy, Holland, and Belgium: branvin in parts of Norway and throughout the rural parts and in some of the cities of Sweden: the use of home grown corn and potatoes for the manufacture of intoxicating liquor is prohibited dm Denmark and other countries: the manufacture of spirits for (beverage purposes has ceased in Great Britain and its sale in parts of Scotland and on certain days throughout the United Kingdom (is also prohibited. The beneficial results are so universal that prohibition is fast being recognized as the true remedy for the world's drink problem.
Mr. Stanley Washburn, the well-known British journalist, has stated in 1916:-"From Serbia to the Baltic there is not a public-house open, and', further, the Order is enforced to the letter: and greater even than that, it is accepted by the entire population."
Denmark:-An overwhelming majority of the people has declared for National Prohibition, and at the General Election in July, 1918, 69 per cent of the elected members of the various Liberal, Socialists, and other parties pledged * themselves to enact a measure for taking a National Plebiscite on Prohibition.
In France, Switzerland, and some other European countries, the demand for Prohibition or more drastic restriction on the liquor traffic is growing louder and more persistent.
I heard one hon. member of this House make the remark a few days ago that the drinking of coffee for a certain time caused sickness and that it was necessary, in order to counteract the effect. of the coffee, to take something stronger, or to indulge in another way. Well, if coffee has such an effect on the individual that it is necessary to resort to something stronger, I think I can prescribe a remedy that would be more effective than that if my hon. friend would accept my prescription. I would say to him that, instead of taking strong coffee to make him sick, and taking strong liquor to cure him, if he would take pure water all the year around, he would have none of these troubles at all. I read the following citation:
Civil War and Prohibition.
The first State to adopt Prohibition was Maine. From 1S51 down to the present time, with the exception of a few months in the years 1856-57, prohibition has been the law of Maine. On March 29th, 1918, the Governor of this State, in an address delivered before the State Convention of the Republican Party, at Portland, Maine, said:	" The honest efforts
of all officials charged with the enforcement of the Prohibition law in Maine have brought about a condition so satisfactory that all discussion of the wisdom of the law has permanently ended." This is surely an effective answer to those who declare that " Prohibition does not Prohibit."
Clearing the Liquor from Government and Civil Positions.
In spite of the powerful influence of the liquor interest and its influential lobbying in Congress, year after year the Temperance Reformers have made inroads upon the various strongholds of liquordom. To protect the In-
169i
dians, a Prohibition Zone has been established round every Indian Reservation. To protect the soldiers and sailors the sale of intoxicating liquors has been abolished from all Canteens, Army and Navy Training Camps and Naval Depots. Prohibition is also enforced in all Soldiers' and Sailors' Homes, Army Reservations, National Homes for Disabled Volunteers and Emigrant Stations, &c. To protect the workers a Prohibition zone has been established round shipyards and Government workshops. To protect young people, the evil effect of alcohol upon the human system is taught in all the public schools, colleges, and universities throughout the land1. By an Order issued September, 1918, the selling of alcoholic liquors is now prohibited on trains and1 at Railway Stations. Railway Corporations and many of the great industrial concerns have, with the approval of the Trades Unions connected therewith, prohibited servants employed by them from drinking while on duty, and in some instances this is extended to drinking whilst off duty, or frequenting places where intoxicating liquors are sold. The great fraternal organizations, such as the Masonic, Trade and Thrift Societies, totalling a membership of over 12 millions, exclude liquor-sellers from membership, and many societies call upon their members to vote for Local No-License and State-wide Prohibition.
Surely, if that has been the experience in the past, we cannot be too careful at this moment in changing the present condition as to the restriction of the liquor traffic, especially when societies representing 12,000,000 people will not admit to membership any one engaged in selling liquor or who is associated with the traffic. 1 read:
Methodist Minister Arrested.
The arrest of the Rev. S. F. Newton, pastor of the East End Methodist Church, for distributing temperance literature on the streets without a permit was one of the incidents of the campaign on Wednesday. Mr. Newton stated that he had permission from the general manager of the Canadian Consolidated Rubber Company to distribute leaflets among his employees.
There is a case where a clergyman trying to do good, and innocently distributing certain kinds of literature, is arrested. We know, notwithstanding it was forbidden by this Government, that certain propagandists were distributing literature, that they were arrested, convicted and sentenced to two or three years' imprisonment, that their sentences were commuted and that they.were set at liberty. When men had been convicted of doing things of this description this Government had no right to interfere with the law but the law should have been allowed to have taken its course. Yet, here is a man,'a minister, who is doing harmless work and he is arrested and put in prison. It is not very creditable to those who undertook to bring about his arrest. I read:

Mr. Brewer: We are absolutely opposed to the restoration of the drinking bar. They propose to cleanse whisky drinking of its relations with crime and vice by changing its posture and ensconcing it behind tables. So universally are vice, crime, corruption, disease and misery associated with the bar, that both brewers and distillers are willing-nay anxious -that it should be banished-if only they can go on doing the mischief they have been doing by means of it. But no change of fittings or of posture is going to change the nature of the reptile or the fruits of its activities..
There are streets in Montreal whose reputation is so bad that their names have had to be changed over and over again. One which was named after a saint had to be unsanctified and was then called after a national hero, but he, in turn, had to be relieved of it; and it was again reduced to a more fitting godfather. It will be the same with the drink trade; its outward form will not change its unholy results.
Then., as to the saloon, we have the following declarations:
Death on the Saloon.
The Committee of Fifty, in their exhaustive study of the liquor traffic in the United States found that out of the unions investigated one out of every five is, by its constitution, directly opposed to the saloon, one out of every three is at least generally opposed to it, while only about 25 per cent of all unions seem to have no definite policy in relation to the liquor traffic;
Now come the opinions of labour leaders, men occupying responsible positions, and organizations of working men:
To inquiries, answers were received as follows :
Order of Hailway Conductors: We are absolutely opposed to the saloon, and it is incorporated in our laws that a man cannot engage in the liquor traffic and remain a member of this organization.
Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen: We oppose the saloon to the extent that the Brotherhood will not tolerate a member being connected with the sale of liquor.
International Seamen's Union: We continually enjoin sobriety upon our members by refusing to publish advertisements of the saloon, etc., in the official organ of the union.
United Garment Workers: Our organization is decidedly opposed to the saloon.
The Journeymen Tailors: The officers of our organization are decidedly opposed to the use of intoxicating liquors as a beverage and its general secretary adds: " I have not failed whenever the opportunity has presented itself, to declare myself upon this question."
The United Mine Workers of America: The officers of the United Mine Workers of America discourage in every respect saloon business.
The constitution of the Telegraphers reads: The use of alcoholic liquor as a beverage shall be sufficient cause for rejecting any petition for membership.
And to crown all, and to prove that the fight against the saloon is not of recent origin, in 1894 the International Typographical Union in its convention called for " the State and national destruction of the liquor traffic."

The Blacksmith's Journal says the greatest curse to the labour movement has been the saloon, and it is high time that the labour leaders got together and forever divorced the trades union movement and the saloon influence.
It is a readjustment, a changed condition of society. Almost every disturbance in the ranks of organized labour can be traced back to some connection with the saloon.-John Mitchell, Vice-President A. F. L.
I have been criticised for my fight against the saloon, but I give notice here and now that I will fight the traffic as long as the saloon opposes the interests of the people. Too many men and women are going downstream to degradation for me to keep silent. To the trades unionist there is no redeeming feature in the saloon. Go anywhere where its influence is felt and you see the demoralization it brings. We are fighting for social well-being, civil benefits, and moral uplift. Never a foul plot is organized to injure public rights and social well-being but the saloon is used for the job.-John B. Lennon, Treasurer American Federation of Labour.
I know that I am right; I know that in refusing to even touch a drop of strong drink I was, and am, right. In refusing to treat another to that which I do not believe to be good for myself to drink, 1 know I am right. In refusing to associate with men who get drunk, I know I am right. In not allowing a rum-seller to gain admittance into the Order of the Knights of Labour, I know that I was right. In advising our assemblies not to rent halls or meeting rooms over drinking places, I know I was right. I have done this from the day my voice was first heard in the council halls of our order.-Terrance V. Powderly, former Gen-tral Master Workman of the Knights of Labour.
I will now give quotations showing what the position of President Wilson is: President Wilson's Glass of Water.
The American press report that when President Wilson responded to the toast of the President of the French Republic in Paris, he raised a glass filled with water, President Wilson drank no wine at the luncheon. Explaining the President's action to the French, Dr. Grayson# hist physician, said that Mr. Wilson never drank wine or alcoholic liquor of any kind.
Here is a further statement showing the attitude of labour towards the liquor traffic: Slandering the Workingman.
Friends of decency and sobriety are getting exceedingly tired of the constant vilification of labour at the hands of the Liquor Traffic. Every time an attempt is made to pass some prohibitory legislation there is a protest in the name of labour. We must not shut down the saloon lest labour be angry and cease work. The curious fact is that every time the vile grogshops have been put out of business in any large numbers, labour, far from quitting or causing trouble, has immediately become more efficient.-Zion's Herald, Boston, Mass.
That goes to show the opinion of the workingman and the effect which prohibition has with respect to his efficiency. Now let me give the opinions of the Canadian provincial premiers in regard to the value

of prohibition. The International Record contains the folowing:
Prime Ministers and Prohibition.
During' February, 1919, an extraordinary expression of opinion on the value of Prohibition was given by statesmen, professional and business men and others. We have only space for the following:

Sir G. H. Murray, Prime Minister of Nova Scotia-"I regard Prohibition in Nova Scotia as very beneficial."
Hon. T. C. Norris, Prime Minister of Manitoba-"Results of Prohibition are certainly beneficial."
Hon. W. M. Martin, Prime Minister of Saskatchewan-"Money formerly spent on liquor now finds its way into more legitimate channels. Crime has greatly decreased, and one of our jails has been closed."
Hon. N. E. Foster, Prime Minister of New Brunswick-"Prohibition in New Brunswick since it became effective in May, 1913, has undoubtedly given satisfaction."
Sir W. H. Hearst, Prime Minister of Ontario

''All parts of the province Indicate the success of Prohibition."
It is apparent, from the statements I have read containing expressions of Oipinion by labour leaders, that it is a libel upon workingmen generally to say that they are not sympathetic towards prohibition. I have also given you the opinions of the various provincial premiers throughout the Dominion, and I think it can be taken for granted that a similar opinion is held by the Premier and the Acting Premier of Canada. Such being the case, and the House having now to deal with a prohibition measure, every clause of the Bill should receive the greatest consideration, and should be put in such a form as to demonstrate that Parliament proposes to discourage rather than encourage the liquor traffic and the consumption of liquors of any description. Surely it will not be long until the day comes when throughout this Dominion there will be total prohibition. I think you will find that every province will eventually vote in favour of it.
I do not suppose there is an hon. member but has had more or less experience of the degradation, the suffering and the wasting of energy of men and women through overindulgence in the use of intoxicating liquors. The world knows by this time that liquor sold under high license, low license, or no license, in saloon, export warehouse, or government grog shop, by hotel keeper, dealer, or " factor," whether across a bar, on a table, or in a sealed package is the same liquor, and it is the liquor that does the damage. Let us not be confused or deceived in this matter. The foe we are fighting is alcohol.
Then I saw the mother shudder and tremble as if with dread,
As she heard on the rotten staircase the sound of a heavy tread,
And the children run to their mother, and cry in their deep despair,
Oh, hide us from our father, for we hear him coming there.
Then I see the door flung open and a form come staggering in,
The form of one God made as man, now a brute through the curse of gin.
Those hungry babes are his children, that fainting woman his wife,
And he was their proud protector till the liquor ruined his life.
Now the stone is rolled away.
Hail the glorious Temperance Day.
