speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I agree with the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) with regard to the turn taken by this discussion and I shall endeavour to confine my remarks to the matter in hand. As I understand it, this is an amendment that will continue the provinces in the right that they now have to deal with the use of intoxicants, I believe that when the Government dealt with the liquor question as a war measure and passed the Order in Council, they did one of the very wisest things possible under the circumstances, and there is no doubt that very great profit accrued to us as a people because of the advantages that followed that measure. The part that Canada played in the war would indicate that the action taken by the Government was along the right lines and brought splendid results. Now that the war is over and we are coming back to normal conditions, naturally the question comes up as to what should be the attitude of Canada on the temperance question. That brings us back to the point as to where the provinces stood on this question previous to the war, and there can be no doubt that their pronouncement was emphatic and conclusive along the line of prohibitory legislation, with the exception of one province, and that province through local option measures had in large measure in effect pronounced against the evils that flow from the effects of intoxicants used for beverage purposes.
I am glad that the Government has brought this matter up for consideration. In the main I agree with the Bill as now presented, which will leave the matter in the hands of the provinces to be dealt with as they see fit. I have always been a believer in provincial rights, and this regulation is placing the matter where the law previously enacted by the provinces placed it. In view of the fact, however, that the Order in Council gave practically Federal prohibition, and that we are enjoying that condition of affairs at the present time, it seemed to me that we might perhaps have left the Order in Council as it is, with the right reserved to each province, if it saw fit, to bring up the issue and vote on
[The Chairman. ]
it, as to whether it would continue a prohibition province or not.
This would have practically removed the question of prohibition as a contentious matter out of the realm of Federal politics and would have left it entirely with the provinces, and the Federal powers would have concurred in the attitude taken by each of the provinces. As the Bill now stands, however, no serious loss can accrue and no serious damage can be done to any one. I am prepared to support the Bill because of the position taken by the constituency which I represent. I have received from my constituency a large number of petitions asking that the strongest possible support be given to the retention of the prohibitory legislation that has been secured. I have further the endorsation of one of the largest organizations in my province, an organization that has placed itself on record year after year for seven years as being in favour of prohibition. I think that organization represents very largely the sentiment of the province from which I come, and I believe I would be acting contrary to the pronounced view of that organization as well as of the constituency which I represent, did I not make my voice heard to-day in endorsation of this Bill.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
It is not my purpose to discuss the merits or demerits of prohibition, although I would say in a general way that restrictive legislation of too drastic a nature, particularly at this time, is not in the interest of the country under the present unsettled conditions. The extremist in any movement is usually a greater hindrance to that movement than a help. I rise only for one purpose, and that is to point out what I consider was an inconsistency on the part of the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) in the statement he made the other day when discussing the resolution that preceded this Bill. He laid down the principle that legislation on prohibition should primarily be the function of the provinces, such legislation to be enacted after the will of the people of the provinces had been ascertained. With that, I entirely agree. If the people of any province say that they desire prohibition in whatever degree they please, then this Parliament of Canada can consistently enact legislation that will ensure, so far as lies within the power of this Parliament, that the will of the people of that province shall be made effective. When the Acting Prime Minister made that statement, he also stated that when the Government of Ontario enacted prohibitory legisla-

tion, he took it that they represented in that legislation the will of the great majority of the people of that province. I do not know upon what he ibased that assumption. It may be, and perhaps it is, the wish of the people of Ontario that they should have prohibition in that province, but, so far as this Parliament knows, there is no indication that the people of Ontario desire prohibition. Indeed, the election ol 1914 would show that prohibition was not favoured. For that reason my opinion is that this legislation is premature and anticipates what this Parliament believes to be the will of the people of Ontario. The proper method to follow would be this: First, obtain your mandate from the people of Ontario-and I refer now particularly to Ontario, because I know very little about the conditions in the other provinces-then, after that mandate has been obtained, this Parliament would be justified in making effective whatever wish is expressed by the people of that province. The Acting Prime Minister, when he stated that he took it that the people of Ontario endorsed the action of the Government of that province, could not have been in close communion with the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell), -because, as far as I know, the only recent expression of opinion that we have from the people of Ontario was that given in the provincial election of 1914. The President of the Council knows all about that, because he was the leader of the Opposition in the Ontario House at that time, and that election was fought on a question of much less stringent legislation. The question was the abolition of the bar, and, as every one knows, the people of Ontario voted overwhelmingly against the Opposition, led by the present President of the Council. From that, we must gather, if we can gather anything at all, that the people of Ontario were opposed to prohibition, and if later on it seemed that opinion had changed, perhaps because of the war, the proper method to follow, before this Parliament interferes with provincial rights, would surely be to obtain a new mandate from the Ontario people. It may be the case that the people of that province will vote in favour of prohibition, but my argument is entirely on this point, that, so far as we know, the people of that province are, from their view as expressed * in the election of 1914, opposed to prohibitory legislation. This was war legislation in the first place, and now that the war is over, the logical thing to do would be to revert to the position as- before the war so
far as Dominion legislation is concerned. Then, when eaph province declares itself by referendum in favour of or against prohibition, as the case may be, it will become the duty of this Parliament to enact legislation to ensure the carrying out of that expressed view. The thought has just entered my mind whether the reason for this legislation is not that possibly some undertaking or promise was given to the effect that legislation of this character would be enacted. If any such promise was given at a certain time, perhaps a year or two ago at election time, we should be told to whom that promise -was given and what the consideration was.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
I desire to say a word or two in support of this measure, (because in the first place I believg the passage and enforcement of a prohibitory law would result in greater good to the people of Canada than any measure we have put upon the statute -book in recent years, with the possible exception of that in regard to the conduct and the winning of the war.
The Government is to toe congratulated upon the courage it displayed in passing the Order in Council, and I believe that the House will toe commended by the people of this country for the readiness with which it is accepting the legislation validating the Order in Council. As we have recognized the right of self-determination by the provinces in this matter, we cannot have total prohibition at the present time, but this legislation approaches more nearly than any heretofore enacted to the objective at which the temperance people have been aiming for upwards of fifty years, and I believe that it will meet with the general approval of the temperance forces throughout the country. Many years ago ;gir John A. Macdonald told a temperance deputation that they would get prohibition (just as soon as they elected men to Parliament who would vote for' prohibition. I think the action of Parliament to-day indicates that the advice of Sir John A. Macdonald is being followed by the people of this country.
Are we wise in passing this legislation? In the first place, it has been asked whether the people of the province of Ontario are behind this proposed legislation. Let me remind the House that the people of Ontario have voted three times directly on this question, when no other issue was before them. In 1894, in the first Ontario plebiscite, there was a majority of 82,000 in favour of prohibition. The second vote was taken in 1898, when the Dominion [DOT]

plebiscite was held. At that time, although there was very great fear on the part of certain temperance workers that a vote in favour of prohibition would put the then Government in the hole, Ontario gave a majority of 39,000 in favour of prohibition. In 1902, when the third vote was taken, prohibition was carried by the province by a majority of 96,000. In 1916, a petition equal to upwards of eighty per cent of the total vote cast at the election two years before was presented to the legislature asking that prohibition be enacted, and following that, the present Ontario Temperance Act was passed. Surely that is sufficient evidence of the feeling of the people of the province of Ontario on this question, and because of that evidence I believe the Government is justified in introducing the legislation now before us.
Further evidence is found in the western provinces. In 1915, for instance, Alberta voted for the widest measure of prohibition within the jurisdiction of the province by a majority of upwards of 25,000; Saskatchewan, in 1916, by a majority of 71,000, and Manitoba in the same year, by a majority of more than 25,000. The same sentiment prevails in the eastern provinces. In view of this evidence of a strong sentiment in favour of the destruction, as far as possible, of the evils of the drink traffic, I think the Government is justified in seeking to validate this Order in Council, and I am convinced that the only serious complaint that will be made is that the legislation is to be enacted for one year only, instead of being made permanent. I am sure that if this Government or the local Government in Manitoba opened the saloons in Winnipeg at the present moment they would be regarded as fit only for the asylum, and the same Is true with regard to Toronto or any other city, where similar conditions might prevail. For the reasons I given this legislation has my heartiest support.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
I am a victim of unfortunate circumstances. I am compelled to break the law against my own will-that is, so far as breaking the rules of this House is breaking the law. I would not have done so, and I shall do so very briefly, but that there are one or two circumstances I am bound to point out in reply to my hon. friend (Mr. Charters). I have put to myself as carefully as I could the question "Do you think that you can honestly vote for giving greater facilities during the twelve months immediately ahead of us than exists at the present time for the drinking of intoxicating liquor, considering all

the circumstances of the country and the serious time through which we are passing?" [DOT] And I have concluded that my duty to the country compels me to answer that question in the negative. I do not think that I could honestly vote for giving any extra facilities for the use of intoxicating liquors during the first period of reconstruction; but when my hon. friend goes on to say that regret will be expressed that the Government have not gone further I take issue with him, and on very clear and distinct ground. He mentioned the province of Alberta. Now, in the province of Alberta the prohibition vote was as large as it was, very largely because of the constant use by prohibitionists of this kind of appeal-it was said to the people most distinctly: " You are voting on what is practically a measure for the abolition otf the bar; you are voting to abolish the free sale of these liquors in public houses over the bar; there is no disposition to interfere with any one's right to use liquor within his own home." I know I am right about that, because that argument was used upon the platform and in private canvass, and it had a very large influence	upon the vote that
was given in the province of Alberta. I do not know about other provinces, and therefore I do not mention them. Now, Mr. Chairman, what position does that put the question in from the prohibitionist's point of view? Good faith would have required that we should again have taken the opinion of that province on the question of importation. The Government in my judgment were perfectly justified in doing what they did as a war measure, and it was put up to them as a war measure by those who held what I venture to call, without any desire to offend, extreme views on this question. So that under the law complete prohibition was arrived at in Alberta by influences brought to bear upon the Dominion Government-I won't say against the wishes of the province of Alberta, because the question has never been submitted by referendum to the people- but against what they voted for at the time they voted on this question for their own particular province.
For that, reason I do not agree with my hon. friend that this question can remain as it is. I understood that what the extreme prohibitionists were advocating at this time was an extension by legislative enactment of the conditions established by the Order in Council, with the added view that the opinions of the entire 'Canadian people should be taken at the end of that time; and that would be the only fair thing

to my province, having regard to the way the vote was taken.
And, I have a shrewd suspicion that the same thing applies to other provinces. However, as I said at the outset of my remarks, which I am sorry are somewhat out of order, I am in- favour of the Government's measure. I am quite sure they have approached this question with a great seme of responsibility, and I am glad to support them in speech, and if there were a vote on the question I would support them in that respect also. Having looked as carefully as I can into the question I for.one should hesitate to take the responsibility of giving greater facilities, for the first twelve months after peace has been- declared, for the -sale of intoxicating liquors than there are at present.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: I understand that the particular subject before the committee is -the amendment of the hon. member for -London (Mr. Cron-yn) by which he purposes to allow the manufacture in Ontario of liquor -of such strength as is permitted in other provinces. Perhaps on a cursory consideration the proposal might seem reasonable, but a careful study of the question will not support -such a view. If the province of Ontario says it is in favour of complete prohibition, that would imply that it is also in favour of abolishing the manufacture of -liquor in that province, because it would be most inconsistent to say that you are not in favour of the sale of liquor, the consumption of which you think is not in the interests of the people, and at the same time that you are willing to have it -manufactured to any -strength permitted by other provinces. If the amendment of my hon. friend from London were accepted you would have breweries all over Ontario manufacturing beer to seven or eight different strengths. Perhaps British Columbia would permit 3 per cent, Alberta 5 per cent, Manitoba 6 per cent, and so on throughout the different provinces; and under the amendment beers of these varying strengths would be permitted to be manufactured in Ontario while the province itself had said that they did not think that the sale of liquor was in the public interest. I do not think that is consistent. If we in- Ontario say that we want prohibition because we believe it is -good for the people, how can we consistently be willing to manufacture it for sale in- Quebec? On the other hand, -if we pass a law permitting the -sale of light -wines of a certain strength-we may do that, I do not know-can we conscientiously manufacture light wines of a greater percentage of alcohol to ship elsewhere?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
In temperance
legislation why should we depart from the principle of equal rights and the same law for all, and special privileges for none? Why should there be a different law in Ontario in this matter from that in Quebec, and why should this Parliament legislate special laws for each province?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
This Parliament is
not legislating special laws for any province. Each province may pass whatever law it chooses, and by the legislation proposed by the Government we ratify and enable such law to be put effectively into force.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: Why not do the same with any other concern?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
We do not want to force laws upon any province which it does not wish, and as regards the liquor traffic , I think the only just and equitable solution of the difficulty is to allow each province to say what it -wants, and so soon as it had the courage to declare its conviction this Act would enable that province to carry its legislation effectively into force.
I think the Bill as it is is the best solution of the difficulty. It is fair to the provinces and to the Dominion.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
I said before that I was in favour of the law permitting each province to manufacture liquor for export to any other province. The Order in Council, taken on the whole, has been quite unnecessary. But as the Government gave a promise a year ago that it would be effective for a year after the war, we must endorse it under those circumstances. When w-e voted on prohibition in Manitoba the vote was two to one in favour of prohibition, but at that time we had the option, as every one knew, of sending to Ontario or Saskatchewan for liquor. That privilege has been cancelled by this Order in Council and has interfered greatly with the comfort of the people of Manitoba. I have heard it said dozens of times-in fact I do not recall having heard anything to the contrary in Manitoba-that if the vote were taken again under existing conditions, liquor not being allowed to be imported into Manitoba, the result would be vastly different and possibly prohibition would be defeated. We are not going to eradicate the liquor traffic suddenly by such legislation or by enforcing total pro-

hibition. Apparently, nothing has so many public enemies and at the time so many private friends as liquor, but very few of the old private friends are ready to say a word in its defence. Total prohibition can not be rapidly advanced successfully. The only member who has thoroughly understood this matter of temperance-and the question resolves itself into one of temperance versus prohibition-is the hon. President of the Privy Council. If he had had his way and were elected in Ontario he would have proceeded, as he said, to abolish the bar. That accomplished, the liquor stores would undoubtedly have been regulated and the business would have been put under Government control. This would have solved the whole difficulty slowly and gradually perhaps but effectively. The pendulum at present is swinging with terrific force and will come back again to probably the same condition that existed before the war. I remember an old Scotchman years ago having said that it was well to make haste slowly, and the same remark applies when dealing with an old established custom like this. Liquor has been drunk since the time of the flood, because we read that Noah was drunk after that great event. It is evident therefore that liquor must have been obtainable before that period. And we also read in the Scriptures that Christ converted water into wine. The Bible teaches temperance in all great things. And in any great reform such as free trade, it has not been achieved with one fell stroke and in the course of one short year. Total abstinence from liquor will not be effected with any great suddenness. What we want is a reasonable compromise. We might consider France and Italy, which have not yet tried prohibition, and benefit by the experience of other nations. England tried prohibition on a modified plan, providing shorter hours and weaker beer. But so much industrial unrest ensued that they had to resume the longer hours open and the selling of stronger beers. Would Russia not be better off to-day with Vodka galore as before the war than she is to-day tattered and torn and bleeding? I am satisfied that all this industrial unrest is the result of restraint that has been put upon the people by the war. Many men were compelled to serve, and many volunteered, and the war meant a great deal to some
55,000	homes. We had the race track abolished and that meant a great deal of pleasure to many people.
WTe have had fuel control, we have had food control and we have had, last but not least, prohibition, which was the straw that 
broke the camel's back and precipitated to a great extent the industrial unrest that we have to-day. No member of this House has had a better chance to see the workmen's homes than I have had in my experience as a practising physician in North Winnipeg. We cannot say that we have any slums but we have some homes which are by no means superb. I have watched these people at their meals in the days before prohibition came into effect. Many people who have come from European countries are fond of their beer *and, a.s they' have so little comfort in their homes, they receive a great deal of stimulus from a glass of beer at their meals and they are not so restless after their day's work. I am satisfied that the elimination of the soothing effect of alcohol suddenly has had a great deal to do with the unrest. If any member of this House, who has been an habitual smoker, has stopped it suddenly, for a week he does not feel as serene and happy as he formerly did about his home or amongst his friends. It has a soothing effect. In every country there seems to be something needed to soothe the nervous system. The soothing effect of liquor and of beer is something that will be missed if suddenly stopped. A friend of mine said: When you stop smoking, do it gradually. You have to stop it gradually just as we have to stop a morphine fiend gradually.
There has been too much fuss about this prohibition business. We all know that the liquor traffic will die a natural death. The older members of the House can remember the logging bees in Ontario to which nobody came unless there was a gallon or more of whisky guaranteed depending on the size of the bee. Thiity years ago at a medical banquet the best fellow was the one who was on top of the table when all the rest were under. That was only thirty years ago; the other instance, that of the logging bee, was probably forty years ago. We do not find anything of that kind at the threshing and logging bees amongst the farmers of Ontario at the present time. Twenty years ago we had the first dry banquet at Trinity Medical College. This is the result of the process of evolution, of gradual education, of the gradual discussion of this traffic. Yet, temperance people take to themselves all the credit for this process of evolution. Follow Darwin's theory of evolution if you wish. That is the process which has been,going on.
I think it is unfortunate that the conditions as they existed in Alberta, Mani-

toba, and some of the other provinces, have been disturbed by this Order in Council which we backed up on the promise of the Government that at the end of the year it should be dropped. I think it would be well to drop it and let the provinces make the best they can of the Doherty Act, which meets all the requirements.
We have heard a lot about the harm done by alcohol. I am satisfied that tea and tobacco are doing more harm in the land to-day with regard to the mentality, the physique, and the working capacity of the people than liquor, because they are more generally used. Fifty million dollars annually is the estimate placed on the tea bill of this country at the present time. I have known people to drink as many as one hundred cups of tea in a day. In the Old Country an Englishman would never think of taking a cup of tea after a meat meal. In this country, prepare tea as carefully as you can-and in many homes it is prepared very badly-take a meat meal and pour that tea down with its tatmie acid, and the food that you have taken must be tanned as brown as the hide is tanned foi the leather that goes into your shoes. Why is it that in the Old Country you find that most of the people are full blooded, while in this country a great many are sallow and yellow? Because they drink beer at their meat meals and avoid tea. The greatest trouble that the doctor has in treating patients in this country is to keep up the standard of the blood. Because of the quantity of tea that is drunk, it is very hard to do that.
The Women's Christian Temperance Union and various organizations are talking loud and long against liquor, but I am sorry to say that a great many of the members of these organizations never had a drink oi liquor and know nothing about it. Would I be justified in giving a lecture on digitalis, strychnine or morphine if I did not know anything about these things? Yet members of these organizations are lecturing people all over the country on the question of liquor. I am sure that 1 have had petitions from every Women's Christian Temperance Union in Manitoba, all drafted in the same way, from the same copy sent out from headquarters.
That brings me to a story that I heard about the master of the Rotunda hospital in Dublin. There was to be a temperance meeting in the early days of the temperance movement, and one of the gentlemen interested in it said to the master of the hospital: We want you to come on the platform. The master said: I cannot make a speech." " We do not want you to make a
speech, but we want you to be there to show by your presence that you are favourable to the movement." Several of the speakers failed to respond and the chairman was forced to call on the master to make a speech. He said: "Mr. Chairman, ladies and gentlemen, I quite agree that bad whisky is a very bad thing, but I am quite convinced that a little good whisky never did anybody any harm."
Prohibition, in so far as it applies to Manitoba, has brought forward an awful crop of bootleggers and stills and the people afe getting bad whiskey, which, as I have said, is a very bad thing. We will admit that during the first year in which we had prohibition crime fell off eighty per cent. The police stations had to hire people to clean out the halls and so on; they were almost deserted. But to-day that condition of things is changed. Crime has-increased all over the country. The excise department has stated that there are probably 500 illicit stills in Winnipeg. I think they have underestimated the number. In every large city in Canada we find the same state of things. They tried to stamp out potheen in Western Ireland for a century, but they have not accomplished very much yet. This illicit traffic, making criminals of people, is going on. I do not know what the outcome will be, but I am satisfied that -if the people had liquor before the Order in Council came in they are going to have it still. There were few bootleggers until the Order in Council was brought into effect and since then there has been no end to them. The people need liquor and they are going to have it. During the influenza epidemic there was a lot of controversy as to whether whisky was beneficial in influenza or whether it was not. Those who had tasted it and knew of it were the ones who backed it up, while those who had never tasted it are most emphatic in their declarations that it was no good at all. They did not know anything aibout it. I might just explain how alcohol operates by saying that for many years in the treatment of tuberculosis we had given creosote in the hope of killing the germs by this means. Take a child with diphtheria, take two swabs from that child's throat, drop them into two tubes and in one of these tubes put in three or four drops of alcohol; in the tube containing the alcohol there will be no diphtheria germs in twenty-four hours, while in the other tube you will have the diphtheria germs develop.
During the influenza epidemic alcohol was the only poison with which we could flood the lungs in sufficient quantities to have any inhibitory effect upon the

growth and development of these germs. That ought to be sufficient proof that there is need for this remedy; and, although I am a temperance man, I would not want to practise medicine during such an epidemic as we had last winter without using whisky profusely upon -any of my patients who were suffering from influenza. I am satisfied that the results of my treatment will compare with those of any other practitioner on this continent, and I used heaps of toxine and whisky. The people need alcohol for medicine. Last winter they had to go to a doctor for a prescription when they wanted whisky, and had to buy say Burke's Irish whisky from -a drug store and pay as high as $7 a bottle. Talk about the high cost of living. Look at the hardship occasioned to the poor in Winnipeg by reason of the high charges made when they happened to need whisky for influenza. I do not want to be held responsible to say who of my patients shall have a bottle of whisky. It is unfair to the medical profession to expect them to do so, and it is unfair to the public that they should have to go to a medical man and pay one, two or three dollars, as some medical men charged, and then pay the prices charged for -a bottle of whisky as was done in some drug stores. That is not the fault of the retail druggists; I know the wholesale druggists are responsible as well. In the drug business, as in all other occupations there are middlemen, and the effort was made to get more money for their work than the manufacturer received for the finished product.
We have already had a referendum in this Dominion on the question of prohibition, and as a boy I worked hard for that referendum. The vote was a very close one, but it did not do any good, and I am satisfied that no federal referendum will achieve any great benefit. I believe the situation in regard to. prohibition should be left to each province to deal with. We have not had success with the law as it applied to Manitoba. I repeat that in the last influenza epidemic the wholesale druggist charged all sorts of prices, and the people were either held up by medical men for prescriptions, or else the doctors did not make any charge; it is distasteful to any conscientious member of the medical profession to be placed in such a situation as arose at that time. My suggestion, and my advice to Manitoba in a case like this, and I suppose the remedy might apply equally to other provinces, is to establish provincial liquor stores under

Government control and sell the best liquor that -can be procured at a reasonable price. License the head of each home, charge a nominal fee of one dollar per year for the license, and then permit the purchase of a bottle of whisky, or a case of beer per fortnight, or per month, as the provincial government may deem proper. In that way the traffic -can be regulated, real temperance brought about, and the tendency to crime removed. Control of the traffic, to my mind, is the important thing. We cannot hope to bring about total prohibition because stills will go on, just as the production of wine has always taken place on this globe. My hope is that people will deal with this question sanely; that they will try and carefully control the liquor traffic and not endeavour to enforce total prohibition immediately.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
L desire to ask the promoter of this measure-I do not know whether the Acting Prime Minister or the President)* of the Privy Council has it in charge-if native wine can be made i-n the province of Quebec up to the same percentage of strength as is made in Ontario under this Bill, and if the same thing can be done in British Columbia or any other -province? The hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) said this was not special legislation, but as 

T read the Bill it is special legislation with respect to province after province. What I want to know is whether wine can be manufactured in Quebec up to twelve per cent strength as in Ontario, and whether the same thing can- be done in British Columbia, or vice versa?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: Yes, if the law of the province of British Columbia permits the sale of native wine for beverage purposes up to that strength. Ontario places its whole limitation upon the strength of the native wine which may be sold in the province for beverage purposes subject to the regulations that are in force.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
The point I want to make is that we are legislating for one province on- one line and for another province on another line, according to the whim of a particular province for the time being. My view is that we should have 'the same law for one province as for another; that there should be a universal statute applicable throughout the whole of Canada. This Parliament has no right to legislate according to the whim of any particular province. If you do that in the case of one

province why not do it in the case of another?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
I want to
say a few words in favour of the amendments to the Order in Council embodied in this Bill as presented by the Government. In the first place I think the measure recognizes fully .the rights of the respective provinces to deal with this matter. It recognizes the legislation of the provinces and also the implied sentiment and attitude of a province where full and final legislation has not been put into effect. [DOT]I think 'that the argument raised in regard to the position of the province of 'Ontario is taken care of in that connection. If the people of that province change their view and express it in their ballots, the provisions contained in this Bill meets that supposed new situation. While the Bill, does not in the matter of the length of time it is to be in operation, go as far as I personally would like to see it go, I believe that in view of the strength of the position taken by the Government in relation to the situation likely to exist in the year that is before us, (as the member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) has already, stated) we can safely allow this legislation to take care of the needs of our developing country, and then permit the people of the Dominion, either through their representatives directly, or through a provincial or Dominion referendum, to express their sentiments when the twelve months have expired. Further I think this" Bill meets a situation which my hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Blake) argued for in the first part of his address, and then argued against in the last part, viz:	the
evolving sentiment and attitude of an intelligent people of our country with regard to a system which-I say it without any passion or prejudice but speaking historically-has grown out of barbaric instincts. Scientific authorities, not old-fashioned grandmotherly temperance agitators, or the narrow-gauge old time temperance agitator from Missouri, are responsible for that statement. I do not think it necessary for us to spend time in discussing the general principles of prohibition at the present moment. I believe that there has been placed before us a fair proposition designed to meet the situation which will exist in our country during the next year.
I would like, however, to notice one or two statements that have been made in this debate before I resume my seat. In the first place it has been asserted that the opinion of the majority of the people of Manitoba, expressed in various ways, is
that prohibtion has proved to be a failure in that province.
I do not wish to deny any of the statements that my hon. friend the member for North Winnipeg makes, but I will simply cite a quotation with regard to an official claiming that there were at least five hundred stills in operation in the city of Winnipeg alone. He was asked how many stills there were, and he replied: " How many stills; how do I know; there may be two, there may be ten, there may be five hundred." That was the statement that official made. However, a false interpretation of his statement was given publicity, and it was afterwards denied by a reliable and broad-minded citizen of Winnipeg. The same line of argument, Mr. Chairman, would have disproved the validity of Great Britain's position in doing away with slavery; there was many a slave bought and many a slave sold after slavery was abolished. But we do not propose to turn back this evolutionary process in the onward movement of an increasingly intelligent humanity, because there are evidences that we all have instincts which at times claim satisfaction in ways that are not good for the majority.
I think that we do well to enact such legislation as is proposed in this Bill, bearing in mind the outspoken demand and request of a great many thoughtful people in all classes of society throughout our Dominion and in many other countries, that we march steadily forward, not interfering with personal rights, where those rights do not interfere with the development of the national life. In regard to the claim made for the use of alcohol in a medicinal wav-although that is not the point before us-I think we would do well to remember that so far as the public consciousness at the present time is concerned, it is capable of changing this way or that. When we refer to other countries, let us not refer to those countries that have not yet developed such a consciousness as is capable of being developed; and when we refer to the dear Motherland, let us not forget that the Prime Minister of Great Britain-whom we delight to honour when the circumstances suit us individually-is responsible for that very, very strong, if not extreme statement of two or three years ago: That Great Britain had three enemies-Germany, Austria, and drink; and the greatest of these was drink.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I look upon this measure as the most important that has been brought before this House, notwithstanding the vital importance of so many measures that we have dealt

with since it has been my privilege to be a member. In saying that, as a prohibitionist I feel that it is not necessary for prohibitionists to justify, or to attempt to justify, prohibition as a means of wiping out the evils of the liquor traffic. The time has come when it is difficult to find any man who would undertake even for a moment to justify the liquor traffic as we have understood it. There are, however, those who will make an effort, that can only be looked upon as the last dying kick of those who, to retain a portion of their privileges, have from time immemorial fastened their tentacles on humanity through the liquor traffic.
This measure deals purely with the matter of giving to each province that which each province by its expressed will desires. Ontario has been referred to as being, one would imagine, the only province that was effected, and that Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island have been overlooked entirely. The argu-'" ment centered around the question in many respects would seem to lead to the conclusion that Quebec and Ontario were the whole Dominion of Canada. They are important parts of the Dominion beyond question, but there are also other parts of the Dominion. This legislation is for all the provinces and has no relation to one province as against the others, but is simply giving to each the right by its expressed will to have what it wishes.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I would feel that it was unnecessary to go any further, because I rose chiefly to commend the Government for what they have done as a distinct step forward in bringing about what prohibitionists look to as the ultimate goal -the complete wiping out of the liquor traffic. But prohibitionists, who are at the same time sane men, do not wish this or any other Government to go faster than the people want them to, and if the people in any province desire a certain standard of liquor as a beverage I do not feel that 1, living in another province, have a right to say to those people, " You must accept something that I feel I should have because I am not living in your province."
But in order that we may not be misunderstood I would like to refer to one or two things that have been said on this question, sometimes in this House .and sometimes outside. I as a man who, I think, can presume to represent working men to some extent, having lived amongst them all my life, want to place the position of the working man in a proper light before

this House and country. A consistent, determined effort has been made to represent the working men of Canada as being in favour of the liquor traffic. I have been, as I believe has every other member of this House, flooded with petitions, all designed to lead us to the conclusion that the working men were not satisfied with what the Government was doing along the lines of prohibition and the curtailment of the liquor traffic. I am not going to question for one moment the bona fides of those who were circulating these petitions nor am I going to question the bona fides of the statement made in so far as they were representing the views of the individuals who were making them. But I am going to question the right of these men to represent the working men of Canada. I repeat, I have lived my whole life among working men, and I think I know something of their sentiments. I am going to give the House an idea of the efforts made to line up our working men and put them in a false position before the country in relation to the liquor traffic.
In doing that, I will read to the House some of the things that were said to organized bodies of workingmen from one end of the country to the other in an effort to have them pass resolutions in their organizations in support of the attempt to induce the Government to continue the liquor traffic. Some organization-I am not going to give my opinion as to what organization it was-undertook a propaganda from one end of the country to the other amongst organized labour, and that propaganda must have cost at least more than $100,000. I do not think the workingmen provided the money, but that is aside from the question. This is the first letter that was sent out to every body of organized labour in Canada. I will read just one or two extracts because the correspondence is too long to weary the Committee with:
So that you will have a complete record of the actual proceedings, we are enclosing a copy of the resolution referred to.
Experience has1 taught that resolutions do not meet their full value unless active propaganda is systematically employed to enforce them.
We are also enclosing a resolution and appeal, together with a stamped envelope, which we urgently request your Local to adopt at the very earliest possible moment. Kindly return to us at your earliiest convenience after your next regular meeting this resolution with the signature of your secretary and the seal of the local attached.
I want the Committee to notice particularly the next paragraph:

The purpose of this campaign is self-preservation. We desire above all things to keep our organization intact, and at the same time to lend our aid and assistance in fulfilling the expressed will of the workers as declared at the convention, who have asked for the privilege of enjoying a palatable and nutritious beverage which is non-intoxicating.
This statement was sent out by the organization behind this movement and it is the organization responsible for the resolutions which have been misused to represent the position of organized labour, that all that was being asked for was a non-intoxicating beverage. These resolutions were sent to every lodge or division of every one of the bodies of organized labour in the railway service in the Dominion of Canada. The first circular and first resolution sent out did not secure a single reply from any one of those organizations. That was followed up by another letter marked "confidential" and stating:
You have received communications in regard to our campaign for permitting the manufacture of a palatable, temperance beverage

Take note of the word "temperance."
-to contain less alcohol than is permitted in the manufacture of beer in the prohibition state of Maine.
We fully realize that your constitution may not permit you to sign the resolution as such, and it is far from our purpose, therefore, to ask you to violate any of your rules and regulations. If your sympathies are with us, if you feel that we are working along conservative, safe and sane lines, we should be very glad indeed, and we would highly appreciate if you would return the resolution to us, merely writing on its face that your constitution will not permit you to sign it, but that you give us your moral support and good will.
And so on and so on. Again that letter was sent to every one of those bodies from one end of the country to the other and with identically the same result-not a single answer from any one of the organized bodies of railway workers in Canada. Not satisfied with the progress they were making, after the lapse of a month, they sent out another letter marked "private and confidential" and beginning "Dear Sir and Brother." This time they were getting affectionate in their appeals to the workingmen of Canada in order to get their support for the liquor traffic. This letter reads:
We have been hourly expecting the resolution which we forwarded to you for adoption by your local.
We realize that only very unlooked-for circumstances of some kind would interfere with your co-operation. We have been so successful in our campaign that our ambition now is to make this appeal practically unanimous. With a little assistance and energy from you, this can be accomplished.
Please do not entrust this important matter to the mails.
Just as soon as your Local has adopted this resolution, please wire it direct to us at our expense.
We are again enclosing you copy of the resolution which we desire you to use.
Again thanking you for any assistance that you might give us, we beg to remain, etc.
This third appeal, couched in the language that I have just read, met with tlj.e same result as the other two-not one response. I have stated in this House before to-day that there is nothing in my life that I am more proud of than my association with the railwaymen of this country. I never was so proud of them as I was when I learned the result of these insidious appeals to organized bodies of labour men in the railway service of this country, that result being that not a single " local " as these bodies are termed approved the effort that was being made to line up organized labour with the liquor traffic.
While dealing with that, I should like to refer to another matter in connection with it just in order that hon. members in contemplating the possibilities of future legislation regarding the liquor traffic in Canada may take it into their consideration. The statutory law of Canada makes it a criminal offence for a man in the train service of this country anywhere, not only to drink intoxicating liquor, but to be found spending his time in one of the places where this stuff is sold. These so-called beer and wine saloons, that are a possibility under some of the conditions that are contemplated in this House, are of such a nature that if a man in the train service of this country is found frequenting any one of them, he cpn he haled before the,court and prosecuted criminally. That may be too drastic legislation, and perhaps it is, but I am going to give the Committee one or two things to think about before hon. members make up their -minds that it is. The men in the train service of this country are not going to he discriminated against very much longer. They have been discriminated against in the enactment of these laws; they have been set apart as a special class. It has been said to them: You are not going to be permitted to enjoy the conditions that the hon. membeT for Winnipeg North (Mr. Blake) looks upon as so very necessary for the well-being of the workingman; we will separate you as a special class. When this question is finally put before the Canadian people to deteripine, the railwaymen are going to demand that they stand on the same ground as every other man in this country. I would ask the hon. member for

Winnipeg North or any other hon. member in this Committee how he would like to go to bed in a pullman car going out of the city of Ottawa to-night with the knowledge that the man standing on the right hand side of that locomotive peering out into the night as he handled the train across the continent, had sitting beside him a jar of this stuff that the hon. member seems to think is so very necessary in order that the workingmen may be in a position to do their work, that, as he says, they may be full-blooded, that they may have the energy necessary to do these things. Or, I would like to ask any hon. member how he would feel if he knew that the train despatoher, in the still hours of the morning between one and five o'clock, had sitting beside him, instead of a pail of tea (which the hon. member (Mr. Blake) condemns so vigorously) a pail of lager beer. Would he feel that that man's intellect was so very much clearer, as the result of the imbibing of that kind of a beverage to maintain his vitality as he performed the most arduous kind of work any man could be called upon to perform?
The very reason why we have these drastic laws'in the train service of this country is because there is not a man in this House or out of it with an ounce of common sense who does not recognize that the lives of the travelling public would be at stake but for these very laws. The common sense of the men themselves, .recognizing that truth, has made them say, in the constitution of every single organization of railway employees in this country, that a man cannot be a member of any one of those organizations if he indulges in the use of intoxicating liquors to any extent whatever. If the Canadian people, when this question is directly before them for the first time, should decide against prohibition, railroad men are going to insist upon standing on their present ground, because if one of their members happens to come under the influence of drink they do not want to be brought before the criminal courts of this country, as I have known railway men to he brought, on the charge of being under the influence.
Let me say one word-and this brings me to the amendment moved by my hon. friend (Mr. Cronyn)-with reference to the manufacturing within a province of something that the province itself says should not be sold within its borders. I can scarcely conceive of a more immoral proposition being put before a body of intelligent men and the people of this country than to suggest that the provinces of Ontario, Mani-
toba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, which say, "We do not believe there should be imported into or manufactured in our province a liquor above a certain strength, because we do not believe our people should drink it," should, for the sake of financial gain, declare, "We are going to manufacture the stuff that we say is not fit for our own .people to drink, and sell it outside of the province, where it will be accepted." I can hardly conceive of a more immoral proposition from any source whatever, than that there should be manufactured within a province something that the province emphatically states is not fit for its own people to use, whether it is liquor or anything else.
Let me add a word or two with regard to the workingman, because after all it is the workingman who is used as the argument in the effort to continue the liquor traffic in this country. I know workingmen's homes, not one, hut by the score, into which the light of heaven itself has come as the result of the measure of restriction we have had in this country already. I can count workingmen by the thousand who were kept down by liquor when the liquor traffic held sway who so long as their money lasted were good fellows, but as soon as their money was gone were kicked out on the street like so many dogs. That is how the liquor traffic treats the workingman.
I should like to give the House just one instance. In 1912 I had in my employ a man from a town many miles from Ottawa, and the only reason he was bank in the lumber woods of Northern Ontario was because he could not trust himself in places where liquor was sold. On a certain morning I received a telegram that this man's .wife was dangerously ill. I immediately despatched a man to the camp in which he ,was working, to get him out as quickly as possible. He got out to the town in which I lived, and in which there were two open bar-rooms, about two hours before the train left for his home town. He had sufficient money to take him home and look after his anticipated needs there, and left my office one hour and forty minutes before his train left. The following morning I got a wire asking that the man come quickly as his wife was dying. I wired that he had gone the day before and should be at home by that time. The next morning I'got another wire, " Where is so and so? His wife has only a few hours to live." I put the case in the hands of the provincial police to locate the man. They traced up and down the line, but could find no sign of him. The very next morning I got

a wire that his wife was dead, and on the following day a policeman found the man in the snakeroom of one of the hotels in the little town of Chapleau where I live. The climax came in June 1916, when that man staggered out of a bar-room in the city of Hull at ten o'clock at night, and the next morning his body was found against a boom of logs near Booth's mills. That is what the liquor traffic has done for the workingman, and that is why the workingman turns a deaf ear to the appeals of tlhe liquor traffic, that he should get behind it and give it his support. Never was I so proud of my association with the railway men of this country when T learned that notwithstanding these three appeals not one single " local," as they are called, in Canada gave them their support.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
I should not like bo remain silent while this Bill is passing through the Committee. If the case which the hon. member for East Algoma lias just recited were the only one, I be-iieve it would be a sufficient justification for the wiping out of the liquor traffic the world over; but the history of Canada, the history of the continent, nay, the history of the whole world affords hundreds of thousands of if not millions of such instances. History is weighted down with tragic stories of that kind. However, 1 do not wish to deal with the question from that standpoint.
The province of Manitoba passed its present Temperance Act about three years ago and it came into effect on the first of June, 1916. As a newspaperman of forty years 'experience, and as a public man, I want to bear testimony on this great issue, and as a Winnipeg editor, I want to tell of the success of the temperance legislation in that province. The almost complete extinction of the liquor traffic in Manitoba has, in my judgment, been perhaps the most profound blessing that has ever been conferred upon the people of that province. I want to dissent from the position and the views enunciated by my hon. friends from North and Centre Winnipeg. As they are both my personal friends, I differ from them in all kindness and with all moderation. I have talked this matter over with all classes of people. I have often discussed it with many old topers in the city of Winnipeg who were tottering to the grave as a result of drink. These unfortunates voted against prohibition when it was submitted to the people of the province of Manitoba, and invariably they have borne testimony
to the view that while they voted against prohibition they believed it was a godsend to the country and that so far as they were personally concerned prohibition was the best thing that had ever happened. I never found one dissentient voice on this question. Could I bring stronger evidence to bear of the value of prohibition in Manitoba than to tell the Committee that crime in that province was reduced to the extent of 80 per cent by virtue of the adoption of prohibition? We had six jails in Manitoba, and after prohibition there was a time when it looked as if the entire six would have to be closed. Three of them have been closed altogether, and the other three have scarcely sufficient inmates to warrant their being kept open. Is that not as strong testimony as could be submitted in favour of prohibition? I believe the people of Manitoba are overwhelmingly in favour of prohibition, and I think that their view generally is that they would like to see total prohibition for the Dominion of Canada. And when the speech from the Throne announced, as I think it did, that a plebiscite would be taken for the entire Dominion - the Acting Prime Minister shakes his head, and I accept the correction. The impression I had was that a plebiscite would be taken, but it appears to be erroneous. However, it is my opinion that it would be a'good thing if we could have Dominion-wide prohibition. I suppose the federal authority is limited by the constitution, and the Dominion Parliament can only go as far as the British North America Act constitutionally enables it to go. That being the position, I am satisfied that the Order in Council was a good thing. After our Prohibition Act was passed in 1916, as we could not prohibit the manufacture and import of liquor, the result was that a string of liquor houses at such places as Kenora, Keewatin and Fort Frances, were established. On the other hand there were fifty-nine liquor houses established in Manitoba for the purpose of supplying liquor to Saskatchewan and Alberta. While they could not sell it in Manitoba they could export it to these provinces. Of these houses about thirty-nine were run by men of alien origin. I think that is creditable, at least to the Anglo-Saxon. In my judgment the bar should never again be allowed to get a footing in this country. As a newspaper man, and as one who has seen a great deal of life in the city of Winnipeg, almost since its incorporation as a city, I have watched the growth of these



numerous and well patronized bars and have seen their extending influence as the years went by. Little bars ten feet long extended to fifteen, twenty, and thirty and forty feet, until finally, before this Act was passed, we had a large number of circular bars taking up all available space possible in the saloons. I have taken many a visitor from the East to witness the spectacle in these bars at five or six o'clock in the afternoon as workers were on their way from work. We saw' hundreds, sometimes many hundreds, at one bar along, almost five deep, clamouring for liquor and pouring their coins over the counter. As a result of the passing of the prohibition measure in Manitoba the money that went over the counters of the bars by incalculable sums every year immediately began to filter over the counters of the retail merchants' stores, and the sale of boots and shoes and women's and children's clothing enormously increased. I am perfectly sure that if any independent man went into Winnipeg to find out for himself what the benefits of prohibition have been he could not find one independent man or woman-and the women have a great interest in this matter, because they are deeply interested in the liquor traffic-who would not bear eloquent and fervent testimony to the substantial advantage of prohibition. It always seemed to me that when the vote was extended to women the question of prohibition was solved. In Manitoba the men carried the plebiscite by a vast majority of two or three to one, and when we had the accession, as we have had since, of women to the ranks of those who exercise the franchise, those of us who believe in prohibition as a godsend to the people, felt that the question was permanently settled so far as Manitoba at least was concerned. The franchise is being extended to women in all the provinces, and we now have this great army of women, who, I think, are almost unanimously in favour of prohibition. And well might the women be in favour of it, for after all they are among the chief srfHerers. It is they and their children who are subjected to the brutalities of drunken husbands, and who -are deprived of the necessaries of life, because the money which should go to support and make them happy has been thrown over the bars. We know how rich and affluent the saloon keepers and hotel keepers as a class generally became in past years as a result of the liquor traffic. It is generally the saloon keeper who has been able to drive about with a - span of fast horses, wearing diamonds and TMr. Richardson. J
fur coats, and living on the fat of the land. It is no wonder that they desire to get the thin end of the wedge in again.
I want to say a word in regard to the administration of the law in Manitoba. It is true my good friend the hon. member for North Winnipeg criticised it, arid said that since its enactment we have had boot-legging and illicit stills and all that sort of thing. Would the hon. member suggest that if we abolished the law against murder we would have fewer murders, because that is the logical sequence of his argument? Certainly not. The fact that crime has been reduced by eighty per cent in Manitoba absolutely proves the value of prohibition. The Liquor Act in Manitoba has been and is being well enforced. At the head of the License Department is a gentleman of splendid character, of known and tried integrity, and the staff of officials who second his efforts have done thir level best to stamp out the evil. Here and there an illicit still may be found, but that will always dxist. In Ireland, although it is contrary to law, they have had illicit stills for centuries. I suppose the same is true of Scotland, and I have no doubt that similar conditions exist all over the country. You cannot absolutely wipe that out, but if the law is as well enforced as it can be-and I can bear testimony to the fact that it is in Manitoba-we bave reached an almost ideal condition of affairs with regard to the enforcement of prohibitory liquor law. Speaking, as I believe, for the vast majority of the people of Manitoba, we commend every movement that this Federal Government may take to enable us to continue, and if possible strengthen, prohibition in that province. Under this proposed Act I take it that the importation and manufacture of liquor can be prohibited in Manitoba. Is that correct? Yes; the Acting Prime Minister and the President of the Privy Council nod their heads. That being the fact, so far as Manitoba is concerned, we may assume so long as the populace itself is sound on the issue that we are safe in that regard. I have no desire to refer to the amendment of the hon. member for London. It has been criticised and it will be unnecessary for me to say anything on that point. But as the representative of a Manitoba constituency, I want to reiterate the statement that the people of that province look to this Government to assist in every way to make prohibition effective, and would be profoundly disappointed if every available measure were not taken by the Government to secure

that enforcement. If I could be assured that any legislation that might be passed here, or any additional position which the Government could take would make prohibition more effective in Manitoba than it will be under this proposed law, then I am prepared to advocate it. I am one of those who, from long experience and close observation of this traffic, firmly believes that alcohol has been the greatest curse that has ever fallen upon humanity.

Hon. NEWTON W. ROWELL: I think the Committee will pardon me for saying that I listened with a good deal of satisfaction this afternoon to the expressions of appreciation and approval of the policy of the abolition of the bar uttered on both sides of the House. I mention this because it indicates the rapid growth of sentiment in all sections of Canada on the important question now under consideration. Not only have there been expressions in the House and elsewhere, but I notice that in a statement issued by the distillers of Canada and circulated among members of "the House they set out:
It was felt that the public bar with its ever-ready invitation to enter, its customs of "treating," its pernicious record of political activity, and in too many cases its dubious management, could only be dealt with by extinction.
The distillers go further and put themselves on record as being absolutely opposed to any legislation which has for its object, directly or indirectly, the restoration of the public drinking bar. When I recall the attitude, so recently as 1914, of the gentlemen who are responsible for the publication and distribution of that pamphlet, and their very active and energetic hostility to the proposal to abolish the bar, I feel justified in accepting this change of attitude as an indication of the growth of public sentiment on
170J
this question. The hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Blake) has intimated that he thinks that the closing of the public bar is the right policy, and that in this proposed legislation we should not go further. I judge that the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) shares the same view, and that he thinks that in the Order in Council which, we are seeking to ratify we are going beyond what should be considered in the public interest.
Mr. MoMASTER: I do not think the hon. member for North Waterloo expressed his opinion one way or the other on the prohibition question from my recollection of what he said.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
He very carefully avoided committing himself, but I think the statement I have made is a fair inference from what he did say. But while that policy may have been a sound and wise policy in 1914, I venture to think that the war radically changed the situation in all the provinces of Canada, and public sentiment throughout Canada demanded more advanced action than the abolition of the bar. That has been shown by the action which the various provinces have taken in legislating on this question. Wherever it has been submitted to a vote of the people, the vote has been overwhelmingly in support of a proposal which went much further than simply the abolition of the bar. As I recall the matter, the province of Saskatchewan passed legislation for abolishing the bar and putting the sale of intoxicating liquor in shops under government control. That continued for one year. Then the Government submitted to the electors of the province the question of whether the sale in shops should continue, or whether it should be abolished. The result was a decisive vote of the people in favour of abolishing the sale in shops also. The question was submitted in Alberta, as my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) has stated, and the vote included the prohibition of the sale both over the bar and in shops, as the terms of the Alberta Act indicates. That was also the case in the province of British Columbia, in the province of Manitoba, in the province of New Brunswick, and in the province of Quebec in the legislation passed there a year ago. Nova Scotia was dry before the war, except the city of Halifax, and legislation was introduced to make the city of Halifax dry also. Prince Edward Island was likewise dry before the war. That was the general situation. Now

the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) has suggested that there is really no evidence that the province of Ontario is in favour of legislation as advanced as that now in force in Ontario and that we should not proceed with this legislation at the present time, but should defer action until an expression of the people is taken in Ontario this fall. May I say that I entirely dissent from the hon. gentleman's conclusion that the people of Ontario have not evidenced a desire in favour of the legislation in force in that province at the present time. The hon. member from Peel (Mr. Charters) has already pointed out the attitude of Ontario on this question as expressed in the votes which have been given in the province from time to time when the matter was submitted to a vote of the whole people. When the legislation was introduced by the Government of Ontario in 1916 I was a member of the legislature and have an intimate knowledge of all the discussions that took place upon it. But while I concede there was some differences of opinion in the House on the question, some members not being wholly in favour of the legislation, yet the Bill passed the House without one dissenting vote. I do not think there could be legislation as important and radical as that introduced into Ontario in 1916, and no vote against it unless public sentiment strongly supported the legislation.

speechtext:
The interpretation I put upon the vote at the time was this:	The
total vote given in the province of Ontario-I am speaking now from recollection-was fifty-two and a half per cent in favour of the Government or the Government candidates. The vote in favour of the Opposition or in opposition to Government candidates was forty-seven and a half per cent. The popular vote was not

fully reflected in the membership in the House, as the popular vote seldom is on any occasion, and there were other factors entering into the contest, as there is in every political contest. You cannot in an election between political parties have any issue decided wholly on its merits. In the vote referred to other questions entered in; all I can say is that to me it was not discouraging. The night after the election I announced that the policy would he continued; and I may be pardoned for saying I am gratified to-day that the policy has been accepted in all the provinces of Canada by men of both political parties. In reference to the situation in Ontario I have one further remark to make, and 3 make this upon the basis of a statement by the Prime Minister of the province. Speaking at the last session of the Legislature on the matter-Sir William Hearst stated that if the men opposed to the legislation, the men engaged in the trade, had desired a vote in the year 1916, he would have given it.
I know that to be the case: If the men opposed to the legislation which was introduced by Sir William Hearst in the Legislature of Ontario in 1916 had desired that it should be submitted to a vote of the electors before it came into force on the 1st of September of that year, he would have been quite prepared to have had the question submitted. But those who were opposed to the legislation recognized that it would simply be absolutely hopeless for them to successfully oppose it before the people. The sentiment of Ontario was so unanimously in favour of the proposal of Sir William Hearst, that those opposed to the legislation would not challenge a vote upon it; and one of the grounds of complaint, and I think quite just complaint, on the part of Sir William Hlarst, was that after he had refrained from giving a vote because these people did not want it, he should have been criticised for putting the legislation into *	.
force without a vote. Now since that time a vote has been given to the women of the province. There is not an hon. member coming from Ontario, if he considers the question of the women's vote in that province, who will not frankly admit that if you take a vote of the men, plus the vote of the women, there would he a most overwhelming preponderance of opinion in favour of this legislation. Others may not think the vote will be so overwhelming, but there will be an opportunity of ascertaining that when the vote takes place next fall. There is no use hazarding a prediction on the point; but I am persuaded myself that

the vote in Ontario on all the questions submitted will be decisively in the one direction; the people of Ontario will answer all the questions submitted to them in the negative. The position therefore when the Dominion Order in Council prohibiting the manufacture of intoxicating liquor and interprovincial trade in it was passed, was this: All the provinces of Canada had enacted legislation prohibiting the sale of intoxicating liquor within their own boundaries, and the law had gone into force in all the provinces save Quebec, where it was to become effective on the 1st of May of the present year. When the Order in Council was passed the Government believed that it had the power to pass the necessary legislation to continue during the war and for the period of one year thereafter. Orders in Council passed by the Imperial Government, under somewhat similar legislation, were made to continue during the war and for certain periods after the war. The great majority of the Orders in Council passed by the Government of this country under the War Measures Act were made to continue during the war and for a certain period thereafter. But more recently the advice of the law officers of the Crown in Great Britain, and of the committee of lawyers of the British House of Cornmons appointed to	look	into	thematter, has been to	the	effect	thatthe legislation would	end	when	the
war came to an end-that is when peace was officially proclaimed. The Department of Justice concurs in this opinion and this legislation has therefore become necessary.
The object of the present legislation is simply to give effect to the intention and policy of the Government, as embodied in the Order in Council, to implement what they thought at the time they had the power to do, but which appears now to be doubtful; that is, to continue this legislation for the period of one year after the war.
The Order in Council as it stands prohibits the importation, manufacture and inteTprovincial transportation of intoxicating liquors throughout the whole Dominion for the remainder of the period of the war and for one year thereafter. Intoxicating liquor is defined in the Order in Council as any liquor or beverage containing more than two and one-half per cent proof spirits. It is quite true, as was stated by the hon. member for London, that deputations waited upon the Government urging that a change should be made in the definition of the
alcoholic content, and that instead of two and one-half per cent proof spirits it should be two and one-half per cent alcohol. The Government was not able to see its way clear to grant that request. The Government did not itself fix two and one-half per cent proof spirits as the definition of what constituted intoxicating liquor; it found that definition already embodied in the legislation of almost all the provinces. It was the definition of intoxicating liquor in Quebec, in Ontario, and, I think, in nearly all the western provinces. Two provinces had a definition covering even a lower alcoholic content, one, I think, being two per cent proof spirits and the other something less; but no province had higher than two and one-half per cent proof spirits as the definition of intoxicating liquors.

Let me give the Committee a statement made by the Premier of Manitoba in reference to the question:
In reference to the recent order passed by the Dominion Government concerning the control of the liquor traffic, it is regarded as very satisfactory to the Provincial Government rendering more effective the Manitoba Temperance Act. It applies the missing link, and will, I believe, be acceptable to the great majority of the people of the province.
I point that out as indicating that the provincial government recognized that our legislation was not sdpplanting theirs, but supplementing theirs, was providing the missing link, which they themselves had not 'the power, as [DOT] they understood the situation, to provide. What was the view of the* Premier of Saskatchewan on this matter, as stated at that time?
The announcement that the Dominion Government, by Order in Council under the War Measured Act, has determined that Canada on April first next will be under a complete prohibitory law has been received with general approval by the people of Saskatchewan. Almost all the provinces of Canada have now in force prohibitory laws which go as far as their constitutions will permit, but it was necessary for the Dominion to supplement the legislation by prohibiting the importation into Canada and by stopping trade in liquor between the provinces. The beneficial effects of our local prohibition law have been of such a character as to lead to the conclusion that Dominion Wide prohibition will better economic conditions, and will also decrease waste, and will so increase the efficiency of the nation that we will be assured of still greater efforts being put forth to see that Canada performs her full duty in the world's great crisis.

It was necessary for the Dominion to supplement 'the legislation by prohibiting the importation into Canada and by stopping trade in liquor between the provinces.
