Aside from the national approval of any measure tending towards the conservation of all food products for strictly war purposes, the
Dominion Order in Council prohibiting the transportation of liquor into any part of Canada wherein the sale is now illegal is the legal complement to the enforcing of the will of the people of this province as exemplified by the overwhelming majority given on the Alberta referendum.

I shall not do so. My hon. friend from London also referred to the large petition which had been sent to members of the House from various labour organizations in reference to changing the alcoholic content which should be deemed intoxicating. My hon. friend from East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) has already dealt with one aspect of that matter, and it is not my intention to go into it. Even as the Order in Council was originally framed, it met with the approval of that very large and influential body of labour, the organizations of railway employees, who waited upon the Government to present their recommendations against any change and in support of the Order in Council as it then stood. My recollection is that the Winnipeg Trades and Labour Council, the Alberta Federation of Labour, and I think the British Columbia Federation of Labour, voted against the proposal to change the alcoholic content. A very serious strike took place in Winnipeg last year, and the strike committee made a public statement in reference to prohibition which was cabled to New Zealand for use in labour organizations there, in view of the vote which was being taken in New Zealand on prohibition. I refer to this statement because it has a very direct bearing on the present situation. They stated that one of the most important and satisfactory features in connection with the strike was the maintenance of law and order

in the city of Winnipeg during the .whole period of the strike. And that this would not have been possible if the bars had been open.

I ask hon. members to stop and think what would be the situation in Winnipeg to-day, with 30,000 men on strike, and feeling running high as it naturally does "when the situation is so critical, if the open sale of liquor were permitted in that city? I ask further, what would be the situation in Winnipeg to-day if large quantities of liquor were stored there and could be broken into? I venture to think that if this measure was important during the period of the war, it is vastly more important during the year that lies immediately ahead of us. We must recognize that we are passing through a very critical time, that there is a widespread feeling of unrest, that men must keep their heads level and their minds clear. We must recognize that the use of intoxicating liquor under existing conditions, or the granting of facilities for the securing of it, might have very disastrous results where large companies of men are on strike and feeling is running high in consequence.
The present Bill validates the existing Order in Council subject to certain exceptions which I shall mention. The existing Order in Council is to continue in force for the duration of the war and for one year thereafter. It has been modified, and modified only-as the Acting Prime Minis-tre has pointed out,-to give efiect to the change in the situation that 'has developed sin-ce the Order in Council was passed, and indeed, since the speech from the Throne was delivered. In the speech from the Throne the Government promised to introduce legislation to validate the Order in Council. At that time all the provinces had legislation prohibiting the sale of liquor. Since then the province of Quebec, by a vote of the people, has decided to permit the sale of beer containing 2-51 alcoholic content, and light wines. The province -of Ontario has also passed legislation to take a vote on the same question, and it has been suggested-I do not know whether the suggestion has been carried out or not-that some other provinces are preparing to take a similar vote.
The effect of the amendment is simply this: That if any province decided by a vote of its people to permit the sale within that

province of any class of alcoholic liquors, then automatically the manufacture and transportation of such liquor is permitted in that province. Quebec has already decided to permit the sale under certain conditions. Automatically, under this legislation, those liquors may be manufactured within that province. If Ontario, when the time comes, should vote to permit the sale of beers of a limited alcoholic content, then the manufacture of those beers in Ontario may commence the moment the sale commences. Automatically, the Order in Council applies. It is not a question of discriminating between the provinces, because exactly the same principle applies with reference to every province of the Dominion.
The amendment of my hon. friend from London is to this effect: That although the province of Ontario does not permit the sale of beer of a higher alcoholic content that two and a half per cent proof spirits, if we should permit the manufacture in Ontario of beer containing a higher alcoholic content, namely, whatever alcoholic content might be sold in any other province it would mean, if his amendment prevailed, the manufacture of such beer might immediately commence in Ontario for shipment to the province of Quebec or for export.

On one occasion when representations were being made to the Government by the grape growers of Ontario we asked for the information and I was surprised to find how limited the quantity was, and how small was the volume of business in native wines in Ontario. Relatively, it was an insignificant trade; there were only a very

limited number of gallons. My hon. friend from North Winnipeg seemed *to think that there was an objection to this Order in Council because of the necessity for liquor in the case of influenza. I am not going to discuss the medicinal or scientific aspect of that question, but I would point out that no legislation in any province interferes with the use of intoxicating liquor for medicinal purposes. My hon. friend also mentioned that the price was excessive and it was urged that there should be some control. I quite agree with that. Quebec and Ontario have both taken steps to curtail excessive prices in the future. Quebec in its recent legislation prov:des for withdrawing the license from the vendor if he charges an excessive price. In Ontario the Government is taking over the sale, and will carry the business through the License Board. Two or three hon. members have urged that the legislation be rhade permanent. The hon. member for Springfield regretted that we did not make it permanent and Dominion-wide, subject to a vote of the people, and other hon. gentlemen spoke of the legislation being province-wide, that is being continued subject to repeal at the request of any province so far as it relates to that province. While these views do represent the opinion of very many people in this country, the Government is carrying out the promise it made in the speech from the Throne by validating this war-time measure for the period during which according to its terms it should continue in force. In the meantime a vote is to be taken in Ontario where there will be an expression of public opinion on the question. Votes may also be taken in other parts of the country. The soldiers will have returned before another session of the House and the whole matter can be reviewed at the next session in the light of all the relevant facts with- a view to taking such action as the public interests may demand. The Government felt in introducing this legislation, modified only to the extent I have mentioned, that it wa^ carrying out its pledge in the speech from the Throne and giving, as I believe, expression to the real public opinion of this country.

speechtext:
I do not wish to take up much time in dealing with the subject in any general way. I do not think that I would have risen had it not been for some remarks that we have heard from some hon. members who appear to think that any legislation that is brought forward now by people who are generally termed

temperance organizations, such as the Women's Christian Temperance Union, which has been so much complained of, and kindred bodies, is liable to increase the consumption of intoxicating liquors. They are opposed to such institutions, and to the friends of temperance, although if their desires were carried out there would be less liquor consumed. The hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Blake) has given the Committee some medical views in regard to the question. The hon. the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) has replied to a portion of the hon. member's address and has shown that this legislation is not intended to interfere with the use of intoxicating liquors for medical purposes. In regard to any other views that he may have expressed, as to the good effects of intoxicating liquors, or as to the absence of any bad effects, let me remind the hon. gentleman that there are others who are quite as capable of expressing opinions on this question as he is and who have expressed exactly the opposite opinion. In the issue of the Ottawa Journal for to-day, I find that one of the reporters of that paper has had an interview with Dr. Saleeby, whom the paper describes as the leading recognized expert on the effect of alcoholism on the future of the race. I will read an extract or two from what he says:
We and you want to see the Dominions populated with British people. But if those people do not exist where are you going to get them?
' This is one of the factors of imperial importance that must be faced.
The decreasing birth rate in Britain means ultimately that there will be no surplus for the Dominions, and then what? The future of this great Canada is bound up in this question of the birth rate of Britain. To go back to the factors in the reduction of the British birth rate, I said that the war was the chief factor, but the war did not cause the steady decline that had been going on for years before.
Belongs to Racial Poisons.
Alcohol, which I hold belongs to a group of racial poisons, is one of the chief factors in this condition, whether a war is being fought or not. Alcohol, it has been proved, has had the most deleterious effect, not only on the consumer in excess, but on his ability to be the father of healthy children; to be the father of children at all. Babies dead and babies incapable of living we have in immense numbers, due solely to alcoholism. Think of the effect on the future of the race. I am not so much concerned with the drunken man. I am, of course, deeply sensible of the fact that he is ruining himself and abusing his wife. But with the children of that drunken man I am vitally concerned. The racial effect of his indulgence is a matter that concerns not himself alone, but the nation to which he belongs.
In my opinion there is no better stock in existence than the Scottish. For centuries the Scottish race has been the fruitful source of
the best of our Dominion's population. My friend Professor Arthur Keith, curator of the museum of the Royal College of Surgeons in London, reckoned that in the war one Dominion soldier in every three was either Scottish or ol Scottish descent.
Scotch whisky in Scotland to-day is arresting the continuance of that splendid breed. The time has come for the Empire to choose which is the more valuable: Scotch whisky or Scotch men.
Empty of Population.
Our Dominions are practically empty of population and with this war we have made ourselves responsible for immense further tracts of the earth surface. We must have men for them. If we are going on with social practices that ruin the race whence will we get the men? It was not worth going on with the war if it is not worth going on with the race. This war has of course had its terrible effect on the fathers of the future but we must not lose sight of the other war against them that is continually going on. Incidentally this need of saving the future fathers of the race led me to devise the helmet which the British Government honoured me by accepting as the standard for its troops and the American Government added to that honour by adopting it for the United States troops. That, however, is beside the point of the evil of alcoholism. Research, data, statistics of every description, conditions as you may see them each day prove the evil effects of alcoholism on the human race.
I put that up in opposition to my hon. friend from North Winnipeg.

speechtext:
I do not know that what my hon. friend has said has any bearing whatever on the authority that I have quoted and I quote the statement of this gentleman as being as good an authority as my hon. friend (Mr. Blake). I have listened to the objections to the work of so-called temperance people and the assertion that their work has had the effect of increasing the consumption of intoxicants rather than decreasing it, and that their opponents are the true temperance people.

We have been told that very often. Those who oppose these organizations pose as the real friends of temperance. I have been watching temperance work for half a century and I have become rather accustomed to the statement. In this connection I am reminded of the saying that there is nothing new under the sun. When I was a boy I sometimes had occasion to travail over the Cruelph-Erin gravel road for a distance of twelve miles. Along that road, according to the best of my recollection, there were twelve licensed hotels. A great many people in those times thought there was no necessity for so many. They earnestly preached the doctrine that some of these licenses should be cut off, the way temperance cranks do. A strong campaign was made along that line but the liquor interests and their friends held that if the suggestion of the temperance workers was carried out it would cause an increase in the consumption of intoxicating liquor. That was the main argument used against the cutting down of the licenses. It was suggested that the congregating of people in fewer houses would result in more drinking. That was one of the first effective reforms that was undertaken along temperance lines in that part of the country. Another early reform was the cutting down of the hours in which intoxicating liquors could be sold. The same argument was used against that-it would increase the consumption of intoxicating liquors. Not a single thing endeavoured to be done for the last fifty years in the hope of decreasing the consumption of intoxicating liquors but the organized liquor traffic and their friends insisted determinedly would have the opposite effect. We were told the same thing in regard to the Dunkin Act, that its adoption would cause an increase in the consumption of intoxicating liquor. The same thing was said in regard to the Scott Act and local option. People who opposed local option said: "Anything in the world but local option; we are prepared to support you in anything at all that will do away with the use of intoxicating liquor, even total prohibition, but don't say local option whatever you do. It will ruin the communities in which it is passed, and will cause an increased consumption of intoxicating liquors." Every man who has been through those campaigns knows that these were the arguments always advanced. The same arguments were put forward when a campaign was started in favour of banishing the bar. We were told that if we banished the bar it would 
cause intoxicating liquor to be taken into the people's homes, that more of it would be consumed, and the young people in those homes would be taught to use it. Doubtless that doctrine was preached in Ontario and all over the country. I know it was preached in Saskatchewan, because before we actually did banish the bar in that province there had been considerable agitation going on on the part of the so-called temperance cranks and marked advance had been made everywhere along temperance lines by reason of that agitation. The same thing is true with regard to every single piece of legislation that has ever been passed with a view to decreasing the consumption of intoxicating liquors; and I think we may say such objections will always be raised. I think the present legislation is along sensible lines. The President of the Council (Mr. Howell) has dealt so very fully with the subject that little has been left for me to say, except this: The duty devolves upon us under the British North America Act, in view of the decisions which have been given with respect to temperance legislation, to pass such laws as will make provincial enactments effective. The provinces, as we all know, have no power to prohibit the importation, the manufacture or interprovincial trade in intoxicating liquors. Therefore, the only authority that can make the provincial legislation as effective as it should be is this Parliament. The only complaint I * have to make with regard to the Bill now before us is perhaps that it is merely temporary and not permanent. However, it is legislation along the right line; we will take what we can get and look for more.

speechtext:
The debate has taken a somewhat wide range, and while I do not propose to speak at any great length I may be obliged to follow the course taken by others instead of confining myself directly to the Bill.
I suppose we can all accept the principle that the aim of legislation should be to make it as easy as possible for men to live right, and as difficult as possible for them to live wrong. We will find considerable more difficulty when we undertake to define what is right and what is wrong. No doubt it is a serious matter to interfere with the personal liberty of the individual citizen; but it is also a serious matter that the physical, intellectual and moral status ol the next generation may depend upon the quantity of intoxicating liquor consumed by the head of the house. That is also a

serious matter and something that we have a right to take into consideration. The State, I take it, is justified in introducing legislation of this kind interfering with the liberty of the subject, when the subject in the exercise of that liberty, interferes with the general welfare of the State and with the undoubted right of other individuals to enjoy a measure of happiness in this world.
The amendment which is before 'the Committee is in the right direction because its general object is to make effective whatever legislation the provinces see fit to pass. I do not blieve the House should go beyond such legislation as the provinces are prepared to adopt, but, in my opinion, it is perfectly logical and right for us to go as far as each of the provinces wishes to go and to pass legislation here which will make effective the expressed will of the people of those provinces. Such, I understand, is the general intention of the present legislation. I am not one of those who feel very enthusiastic about the Dominion Alliance, nor am I disposed to throw many bouquets at that organization. I think the Dominion Alliance has on a great many occasions taken a course which could not be regarded as a straight course. From 1878 down to 1896, the Dominion Alliance hounded the life fairly out of the Conservative Government at Ottawa by its demands for prohibitory legislation, and from 1896 down to 1911 was practically silent in regard to prohibitory legislation so far as it could be enacted by the Dominion Parliament. The Alliance became active again, especially active, immediately after 1911. I do not agree with some gentlemen who seem to think that the argument in regard to prohibition is all on one side. I think I could produce figures here to show that that is not true in the prohibition States on the other side of the line, bearing in mind what is disclosed by the years 1888 and 1893. It may be said that that is ancient history, but those are the years for which I have figures concerning the prohibition States of Maine, Kansas and Iowa. Comparing those States with the non-prohibition States of Michigan, Nebraska and Minnesota, there were more arrests per thousand of the population for all offences against the law in the prohibition States referred to than there were in the non-prohibition States. There were also more arrests for drunkenness in the prohibition States than in the non-prohibition States, and a greater degree of pauperism in the former States than in the latter. I do not think we would be justified in taking that data as an argument against
prohibition. The figures cannot be regarded as an argument against prohibition because they did not really have prohibition in the so-called prohibition States. Prohibition has never had a fair trial in any of those States. The Royal Commission appointed by the Canadian Government in 1893 to inquire into the liquor traffic examined one hundred and eighty-four witnesses from the states of Maine, Kansas and Iowa. Twenty-four of them stated that the prohibition law was enforced; one hundred and fifty-four that it was not enforced; and six of them expressed no opinion on that point. The report of the Canadian Commission contains this 'Sentence:
The whole trend of the evidence only proves this much, that prohibition prohibits where no one wants intoxicating liquors, but nowhere else.
That was the summing up of that commission in regard to the way in which prohibition was working out on the other side of the line. But notwithstanding that summing up there is undoubted evidence that not only in the United States but in the countries of Europe wherever prohibition has been tried it has been an unquestioned success in the rural districts.
I was very much interested in reading a work compiled by two English gentlemen appointed by the Imperial Government for the express purpose of inquiring into this whole business, Messrs. Rowntree and Sherwell, who have probably written the most comprehensive and logical book that was ever attempted on the temperance question. They spent several years on the work and visited the different countries of Europe, the United States and Canada, and their facts and deductions are well worthy of consideration. Referring to the Gothenburg system in Sweden, they state that in 1900 the consumption of spirits per head of the population was not over one-third as much as fifty years before. At the beginning of the nineteenth century the Swedish government enacted a law which gave the right of distillation to any person who owned or cultivated land. The result was the establishment of 173,000 distilleries, or one for every seventeen of the population, and the drunken degeneracy of the people. Drunkenness was carried to such an excess that, I presume, it disgusted public opinion and led to the adoption of the Gothenburg system. An attempt was made through that system to lessen drunkenness, and by 1895 the number of distilleries had decreased to only 132. The Gothenburg system has

been a very great success if viewed from the standpoint of the amount of liquor consumed per head of the population, but its weakness lies in the fact that while the sale of liquor is under the control of the State, the money received by the State from the sale is used as a means of increasing the local revenue, and consequently the people have an interest in retaining the liquor traffic because the revenue derived from it lessens their burden of taxation.
Now, Sir, I want to name what I consider to be the three principal causes of intemperance, and then to suggest what I think, if not a complete remedy, is something which commends itself to me as more likely to be effective than anything I have heard suggested. First, in regard to the cause of intemperance. What are they? The first is the element of private gain. General Neil Dow, who took such an active part in the prohibition movement in the state of Maine, made use of these words:
The liquor traffic can never Ibe put down so long as there is any profit remaining in it.
That is to say, his idea of the first requisite was to eliminate private profit from the sale of liquor. I believe that that is logical and sound. So long as any persons are making money out of the sale of liquor, there will always be some who will actively" work for the continuance of the traffic. Another cause of intemperance is the monotony and dullness and, too often, the actual misery of many lives. I know there are some who are of opinion that drink is the cause of poverty. No doubt drink is responsible for a measure of poverty, but I think I am right in saying that if it were possible to eliminate all liquor from the Dominion, so that no person could procure any drink for beverage purposes, you would not thereby eliminate all poverty. Drink is not the only cause of poverty. I grant that drink may be taken to be one of the causes of poverty, but perhaps it is not the main cause. Poverty, I think, may be characterized as a sort of industrial disease, and you will have it in this or any other country until industrial conditions have very much improved over what they are at the present time. Another cause of intemperance i3 the absence of adequate provision for social intercourse and healthful recreation. That brings me to the suggestion which I desire to make, and which, perhaps it may be said, has not any direct bearing on this legislation now before us. Reforms, it seems to me, must be constructive as well as restrictive. If we are going to have liquor sold in any province, I think the State

should handle the sale-that it should be a State monopoly. There should be a system of local restriction and control, and if we are to be consistent we must cut out the State profit in liquor just as we would eliminate individual profits in the business. Therefore I say that any profits which arise from the sale of liquor by the State should be used to provide counteracting influences to provide some forms of healthful recreation, some attractions to draw the people away from the place where liquor is sold.
That principle has been recognized in many places in England, Scotland and Wales; it has been recognized in many places in Norway and Sweden, and it has worked with splendid success. Rooms have been provided where the men can meet, have social intercourse, enjoy games and recreations, and the money required for providing those places was the money obtained from the sale of liquor. I commend that suggestion to this committee, and in OTder to give point to that suggestion, may I be permitted to place on Hansard a few words from the pen of Mr. Robert Blatch-ford, who, writing in regard to conditions in certain parts of London, stated:-
Imagine for a moment the common lot of our London poor. Ignorant and untrained minds, weary and unhealthy bodies, gloomy and demoralising environment, monotony and weariness of life, out of these evils spring the seeds of vice. Drudging in their vile stews day after day, night after night-always with the black future like an ominous cloud, casting its chill shadow on their anxious hearts; always with the mean walls hemming them in, and the mean tasks wearing them down, and the mean life paralysing their sick souls ; with no pleasure but drink, with no club but the public house, with work precarious and wages low, in hateful and cheerless surroundings, and with faint hopes ever narrowing, the toiling millions bring their worn bodies and bewildered souls to fight against the devil and all his works-and the devil, amongst other weapons, uses gin. Out in the horrible East the women drink. What wonder! if you go amongst these poor women you will feel suddenly stricken old. What culture have these poor creatures ever known? What teaching have they had? What graces of life have come to them? What dowry of love, of joy, of sweet and fair imagination? Think what their lives are, think what their homes are, think of the darkness and confusion of their minds and then say, is It a marvel if they take to gin?
I place that quotation before the Committee because I think it has a very direct bearing upon two things to which I have previously alluded, one being the fact that poverty is not entirely due to drink, but is largely a result of wrong industrial conditions. But we find, it seems to me, in those words, ample justification for the adoption of any means which will lessen the evil of

intemperance. Notwithstanding what I must regard, from my reading of statistics, as the failure of the attempt at prohibition in the United States, at least in so far as applies to urban centres, I find in the success which attended their efforts in the rural communities very great encouragement for Canada, because this Dominion is largely rural as yet, although there is a tendency towards the cities. I do not mean to say that any law on prohibitory lines which was successful in the rural parts hut a failure in the urban centres is a complete success; it must succeed in both the urban centres and the country districts to be a complete success. But because our population is largely rural, I believe that there is a good opportunity for a greater success of any temperance measure in this country than has attended similar measures in any other country in the world.
I do not believe that legislation in Ontario or in this House is due entirely to temperance sentiment in Ontario or in this House. I believe it is largely due to the fact that it is supposed to be and is, unquestionably, a popular measure at this time. As has been stated by some hon. gentlemen, the position taken in Ontario at the present time is a most inconsistent one. Ontario prohibitionists hold up their hands in holy horror at the thought of any man drinking beer of a greater strength than 2* per cent, but our friends are quite ready to allow a man to drink wine of a strength of 10, 15 or 20 per cent, so long as it is made from Ontario grapes. Ontario says in effect: It is a crime and a shame for a man to get drunk on beer, but it is quite permissible for him to get drunk on wine so long as the wine is made in Ontario and of Ontario grapes. That is an inconsistent position and shows that some temperance agitators in Ontario are not prepared to go as far as they would like members of this House to go in matters of prohibitory legislation. Again, I say the only safe and proper way for us to take here is to go no further than each province is prepared to go. We have no right to force upon Quebec, for instance, the views which may obtain in Ontario or Manitoba, and we have no right to force on Manitoba the views of the majority of the people of Saskatchewan. But we are quite safe in passing legislation here which will make effective any attempts of the various provinces along temperance lines.

I desire to say a few
words in favour of the Bill before the House,
in the firsit place, because I come from a province which has taken the lead and is the foremost province in Canada to-day as regards prohibition legislation, and second, because I myself am a temperance man, that is, I have been a total abstainer all iny life. I am, therefore, pleased to give my feeble word in support of any temperance legislation. I think the Government are to be congratulated on having brought in a Bill to give legislative sanction and statutory enactment to the Orders in Council, and also because they have made this legislation adaptable to the conditions of the different provinces. Whatever prohibtion legislation the different provinces may have will not be interfered with; on the contrary, this Bill will so adapt itself as to meet their wishes and enactments in that respect. It is, therefore, most commendable legislation. Within the last few years there has unquestionably been a great advance in temperance sentiment throughout the Dominion, and it is pleasing to know that such is the case. After all, we cannot make men altogether temperate by legislation, because true temperance is a moral virtue; but all legislation that tends to bring about temperance and that will lessen temptations and remove dangerous occasions from those who may have a weakness for intemperance, is good for the uplifting of the people.
Any legislation that will promote temperance will improve the moral welfare of the community. A good many stories have been told by hon. gentlemen of the evils of intemperance; we have all encountered cases of this kind. The hon. member for East Al-goma told of a man in his employ who was called home to the death-bed of* his wife, but who instead of going home went to the tavern and got drunk, and finally met his death through drink. It occurred to me, while my good friend was telling his story, that he would have performed a good and meritorious act if, knowing the man's weakness, he had kept him in his office for the two hours the man was waiting the train, and my bon. friend might even have accompanied him to the station and seen him on board the train. He was not obliged to do that, of course, he is not his brother's keeper; but I could not help thinking that if he had done so, it would have redounded to his everlasting credit.
I shall not deal at greater length with the Bill because the matter has been pretty well discussed. I most highly commend the Government for the action they have taken, and the way in which they have

framed this legislation to meet the requirements of the different provinces. The legislation will have no effect so far as my own province is concerned, because at the recent session of the legislature the provincial prohibition Act was amended so as to place the sale of liquor in the hands of the Government. We have gone further in the matter of prohibition than any other province in Canada, I believe.

speechtext:
Before you put the motion, Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words in reply to those two members, excluding the President of the Privy Council, who alone touched on the question of the amendment. So far as I was able to follow the speeches this afternoon, I heard only two criticisms directed against the amendment I proposed.
In the first place, the hon. member for -East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) called it an immoral proposition. Well, it is always easy to call a thing names, and even outside of the legal fraternity it is not an unknown exercise of wit by pinning a bad name to a man or an argument, to endeavour to put him or it out of court. But I would ask you for a moment to analyze just what this " immoral " proposition is. The whole proposition is founded on the rights of the province of Ontario or any other province to legislate on this matter of prohibition, and my contention is that the Order in Council and the Bill as drawn do not recognize the Ontario law. If I am right in that contention, my amendment simply seeks to implement or follow the Ontario law, and if there is any immorality in the proposition, that immorality rests upon the Government of the province of Ontario. I understand that my hon. friend from East Algoma was, and perhaps is, an ardent supporter of that Government, and I call his attention to the fact that not merely the export of three per cent beer, but the export of any kind of intoxicating liquor, was permitted under the Ontario Act. That is made abundantly clear by the sections which I read this afternoon. I suppose my hon. friend from East Algoma, if my "doxy" did not agree with his, might call me heterodox; and so he may call a proposal to export three-per cent beer " immoral." But let us look a little further. The state of Maine has been mentioned during the debate. It has had prohibition for something like sixty years, and the statement is made, and I think has not been contradicted, that for many years the state of Maine has accounted beer containing three per cent alcohol by

weight a non-intoxicant. Would Maine then think that the drinking of beer containing two and-a-half per cent alcohol by weight was " immoral?" Would the province of Quebec consider it an "immoral" transaction to drink beer containing two and-a-half per cent alcohol by weight if the same were made in Ontario and exported to Quebec?
Something has been said about the progress of temperance in Denmark and Sweden. Now, in Denmark, as in Maine, the Government declared beer containing three per cent alcohol by weight a nonintoxicant, and removed all duties thereon. The temperance societies in that country, large and powerful, established cafes and restaurants throughout the country and placed this excise-free three-per-cent beer on sale. They believed that to be a good move; they believed it to be in the interests of temperance, and the result is shown by the figures. You will remember that there is no general prohibition law in Denmark. The figures show that in consequence of this move the sale of three-per-cent beer went up in a most tremendous fashion, and the sale of ardent liquors decreased in a similar way. So, I think it cannot fairly be argued that this particular amendment-and no other result is possible in the time in which this law will last- is immoral.
The hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) suggested this case: Suppose, he said, Ontario voted to go completely dry, to allow no sales of beer of any kind; how strange and illogical it would be to allow the export of three-per-cent beer into Quebec. That is a striking supposition, but quite an impossible one. This legislation will last, at the outside, for fifteen or sixteen months'-until peace is declared and one year thereafter. The people of the province of Ontario are to vote next autumn on the question of the continuation or otherwise of the Ontario Temperance Act, and under no possible combination of circumstances, on no vote that can be given on that Act, can the province of Ontario go absolutely " dry." So that the danger conjured up by the member for North Grey does not apply in this case. At the present moment under these very Orders in Council the breweries can export to licensed vendors anywhere, so that whether Ontario went "dry" or not that export business could continue. The President of the Privy Council pointed out the genesis of the Ontario Temperance Act, and I am not at all in a position to argue or contradict him in that respect. He said

that this Act followed generally the Macdonald Act of Manitoba and that the clauses permitting export and transportation were put in to avoid any question of jurisdiction or any attack in the courts as to the constitutionality of the Act. I would like, however, to call the attention of the Committee to one clause of the Ontario Temperance Act which I did not read, as I did not think it dealt with the matter before the Committee, but which is in * striking contrast to the clauses I did read.
I would suggest that this clause is the type of clause which the Government would insert in an Act so as to prevent any possible question as to constitutionality, whereas the other clauses are of a wholly different type, and are framed, I submit, for quite another purpose. Clause 139 reads:
While this Act is intended to prohibit and shall prohibit transactions in liquor which taka place wholly within the province of Ontario, except under license or as otherwise specially provided by this Act, and to restrict the consumption of liquor within the limits of the province of Ontario, it shall not affect and is not intended to affect bona fide transactions in liquor between a person in the province of Ontario and a person in another province or in a foreign country, and the provisions of this Act shall be construed accordingly.
This is a clause such as one could well imagine the Government inserting, out of an abundance of caution, to protect the constitutionality of its Act. But clauses 43, 45 and 46 are on an entirely different basis. They deal with the right of common carriers to carry liquor for export, and the right of the manufacturer to sell for export. The President of the Privy Council said, in answer to a question by an hon. member, that the test of the right to export is the right of sale within the province. That is the test as matters stand today. Under the Bill which the Government has introduced you can export wine of Quebec strength into Quebec because Ontario allows the sale of that wine. But as I pointed out in moving the amendment, if Ontario next September allows the sale of beer of 3 per cent or 2i per cent alcohol by weight-if it follows the Quebec lead in that respect-even then, when the sale of that beer is allowed in Ontario, under this Act as brought in, that beer could not toe exported into Quebec nor could beer be imported from Quebec. So that the sale test is only partly applied and unless the amendment which I suggest is adopted there will be that defect, that illogical position. I desire to repeat briefly what the general effect of >my amendment
is: It. allows the manufacture in Ontario of beer of a strength which is permitted to be sold in Quebec, and the export of that beer to Quebec or any other place where it may lawfully be sold.
Amendment (Mr. Cronyn) negatived.

speechtext:
COMPULSORY RETIREMENT OF OFFICERS AND MEN. *
On the motion of Major-General Mewburn (Minister of Militia and Defence), the House went into Committee on the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the Militia Pension Act, chapter forty-two of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, and to pro vide:-
1.	That an officer who is retired compulsorily, for any cause other than misconduct or inefficiency, after ten years' service, shall be entitled to a pension for life, not exceeding one-fiftieth of the pay and allowances of his rank or permanent appointment at the time of his retirement for each completed year of service.
2.	That in the case of an officer who has been seconded or given leave of absence for service in a position in the public service of Canada or in the Canadian Expeditionary Force or in any other military force raised in Canada for service outside Canada, and paid and maintained by the Government of Canada, or who has been permitted to serve in any such force, deductions at the rate of five per cent per annum shall be made from the salary or pay, as the case may be, which such officer is receiving in the said public service, or as an officer in any such force, and those deductions shall form part of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, and shall be treated in all retepects as deductions under section eight of the Militia Pension Act; and, notwithstanding anything in that Act mentioned, the pension granted to an officer thus seconded, or thus serving in any such force, shall be based on his salary and allowances, or his pay and allowances, as the case may be, which at Ihe date of his retirement the Said officer is receiving from the said Government in the public service or in such force.
3.	That the time served as an officer, noncommissioned officer or man on active service during the war between Great Britain and Germany, which commenced on the fourth day of August, one thousand nine hundred and fourteen, shall be counted for pension purposes under the said Militia Pension Act.
4.	That every militiaman shall be entitled to retire and receive a pension for life who has completed not less than ten years' service, subject to the provisions of the Militia Pension Act.
5.	That the pension to a miilitiaman on retirement shall be:-
(a)	if he has completed ten but less than
twenty years' service, an annual sum equal to

one-fiftieth of his annual pay and allowances for every completed year of service;
(b)	if he has completed twenty but less than twenty-five years' service, an annual sum equal to twenty-fiftieths of his annual pay and allowances, with an addition of two-fiftieths of his annual pay and allowances for every completed year of service above twenty years;
(c)	if he has completed twenty-five years'
service, an annual sum equal to thirty-fiftieths of his annual pay and allowances, with an addition of one-fiftieth of his annual pay and allowances for every completed year of service above twenty-five years:	Provided
that tht pension shall not exceed two-thirds of his annual pay and allowances at his retirement.
6.	That the time served as a militiaman on active service during the war between Great Britain and Germany, which commenced on the fourth day of August, one thousand nine hundred and fourteen, shall be counted for pension purposes under the said Militia Pension Act.
7.	That the Governor in Council may as to him seems fit grant a pension to the widow and a compassionate allowance to each of the children of any officer who, having completed twenty years' service, was at the time of his death on full pay, or who, having completed ten years' service, was at the time of his death in receipt of a pension.
8.	That the pension of a widow shall, if her husband was at the time of his death on full pay, be an amount equal to one-half of the pension to which he would have been entitled if he had been retired compulsorily immediately before hie death, or, if at the time of his death he had been pensioned, an amount equal to one-half of such pension.
9.	That pensions to widows heretofore granted under the provisions of the Militia Pension Act may be re-adjusted in accordance with the provisions of these resolutions; but no saich re-adjustment shall authorize the increase of any payments for pension that accrued before the passing of the Act based upon these resolutions.
Major-General MEWBURN: The object ol this resolution is to carry into effect one or two amendments in the old Militia Pension Act, which now provides for compulsory retirement after twenty years' service. Under the old Militia Pension Act an officer or a man could' only be pensioned compulsorily after twenty years' service. This amendment permits the pensioning of officers after ten years' service instead of twenty. It will enable us to pension certain officers instead of keeping them on the strength for twenty years; especially the large number of officers promoted from the ranks who have served overseas during the present war, and who cannot be absorbed in the establishment. The second resolution makes provision in connection with officers of the permanent force who have been seconded, or given leave of absence in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, or other military forces. The Pension Act only provides for officers 171*
seconded in the public service in Canada - and, by adding the words "Canadian Expeditionary Force," it will enable us to pension officers of the Permanent Force who have been promoted from the ranks, or officers of the Permanent Force who have been promoted to a higher rank in the Canadian Expeditionary Force. The present Act, of course, was passed without any thought of this war. This does not provide for voluntary but compulsory retirement. It provides for the recognition of war service and makes it unnecessary for officers and men of the Permanent Corps who distinguished themselves in the war to return to their lower ranks. It would be manifestly unfair to require non-commissioned officers and men who have distinguished themselves to revert to their rank as non-commissioned officers and men. In connection with section 3 of the resolution, I might also refer to section 6 which provides that the service of men in the recent war will be considered towards pension. Under the old Militia Pension Act provision was made for men who had served in the South African war or the Yukon. Iln accordance with the precedent .created after the South African war this section enables us to count towards pension the time that officers, non-commissioned officers and men have served in the Canadian Expeditionary Force. 'Section 4 provides that the men are to be pensioned on the same ratio as the officers. It also gives the right to a man, which the officer does not possess, to retire voluntarily at the end of ten years service. Section (5) subsection (a) provides that militamen can be pensioned after ten years' service. Subsections (b) and (c) of section 5, are the same as now provided in the Act, except in the addition of the word " allowances."

Major-General MEWBURN: In the interpretation clause "militiaman" means a non-commissioned officer or private of the force. All ranks below the commissioned rank of lieutenant would be included in the word "militiaman" under that interpretation.
Sections 7, 8 and 9 are identical with the Royal Northwest Mounted Police Pensions Bill which went through the House last week. Section 7 simply provides for the reduction of time from twenty years to ten years, in which time a pension can be granted to a widow, provided her late husband was in receipt of full pay or pension.

Section 8 is identically the same as the Mounted Police pension. It provides that the widow of a husband if he were, at the time of his death, drawing full pay, should receive equal to one-half of the pension to which he would have been entitled. Section 9 makes provision identically the same as under the Mounted Police pension, that is, the pension of widows already granted under the provisions of the old Act, can, by Order in Council, be readjusted from the date of the passing of this Act.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: For example, the liners that come in from Boston or any other port will only have to pay on two occasions each year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: That is the meaning of it.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: What is the reason for the change? Is it because the present dues are insufficient to pay the harbour master?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
That is one reason; and the other reason is to enable the harbour master to draw more than $1,800 from the fees collected. For instance, in

the year 1915 he was only able to collect in fees $1,714, which really is too small an amount for a man who has the responsibilities of harbour .master for a port like Halifax.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: How much did he collect last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: That was a very large year, $3,351. But the harbour master stands no show whatever of getting an income beyond $3,000, because the war is over and the amount of shipping going in and out of the port of Halifax will not be so large that he will be able to draw such a salary, but he certainly will draw more than $1,800-1 hope he will, anyway.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: Has the Board of Trade or any other body at Halifax asked to have these changes made?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: No one has asked it as far as I know. It is just a matter of what the minister would consider fair and just in the way of remuneration, and I think that a harbour master who has been in the service for thirty-four years, considering the high cost of living, would not be treated fairly if the Government only gave him $1,800 a year. I am sure hon. members will agree that if he can collect more fees than $1,800 he certainly ought to be entitled to them.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: I agree with the hon. minister that $1,800 for the harbour master of Halifax is not sufficient remuneration, and I think the vessels can afford to pay the fees laid down in the resolution.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: How are those fees collected ?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: At the custom house, are they not?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: I presume so.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: This will be an amending Act, I understand ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: I should like to have it clear that those fees are collected at the custom house. I do not like the idea of an officer going aboard a ship arid collecting fees for himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: That is the way it is done.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: Does that official fall within the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: He is under the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
Yes.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. BALLANTYNE thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 119, to amend the Acts respecting the appointment of a harbour master at the port of Halifax.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext:
On motion of Hon. Newton W. Rowell (President of the Council), Bill No. 116, to amend the Royal Northwest Mounted Police Act, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 9-those who left Force to serve in war on rejoining Force, service in war to be included in computing pension:

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Are there many who joined the forces?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Yes, -several hundreds
went to the war.

Section agreed to.
On section 10-rates of pay:

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: How will this rate of pay compare with the previous rate?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
This rate of pay was the rate established by Order in Council last autumn when we decided to recruit the Force up to the authorized number of 1,200 men. The rate iS" 50 cents -per day for constables and non-commissioned officers above the rate of pay that prevailed before the war. It is only right here to mention to hon. members that, as was suggested when we were discussing the resolution, the rate of pay during the next two or three years will have to be increased above this amount, and provision for that is made in the latter
part of the section by giving the Governor in Council power to do so. I think the rate of pay of constables will -have to be 50 cents per day above the amount fixed in the Bill which will make the constables start at $2 a day. It is not possible, we think, to get the most desirable men and to recruit up to strength unless we make the pay for the next three years start at $2 per day. We should also increase the pay of non-commissioned officers by 75 cents per day and the officers by $1.25 per d-ay.

Section agreed to.
On section 11-creation of a reserve of officers and men who have served in Force.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I desire to make a slight amendment in this clause. Members of the Committee will see that subsection 3 reads:
When such officer or man ot the said Reserve shall have been called up for duty he shall hold the rank and draw the pay which he received on the date of his retirement or discharge from the Force.
We should make that read "current rates of pay when he is called up." I therefore move to amend the clause by striking out all the words after the word "rank" in the second line and -substituting therefor the following:
"Which he held on the date of his retirement or discharge from the Force and shall receive the current rates of pay for such rank.
Amendment agreed to.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Subsection (7) of this section reads:
Any member of the Reserve may retire therefrom on giving one month's notice in writing to the commissioner.
Does this extend to the man who is called for service, because that would be most acceptable?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No, this reserve applies only to men who have served their full period in the Force and have retired or been discharged. It provides for creating a reserve of retired men who have served in the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. They cannot be brought in unless they voluntarily consent to do so, and if once they are brought into the reserve and called for service, they may retire on a month's notice.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Subsection 2 says:
Such reserve, or any portion or member thereof, may be called up for duty by the Commissioner when he deems it necessary.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
They must be enrolled in the Reserve, then they may be called up

for duty. After a man has been called up for duty and is serving, he may give notice that he wishes to withdraw at the end of the month.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: In that case would he receive both pay and pension? These men forming the reserve are presumably pensioners, and in emergency they may be called out. They would receive the pay of their rank at the time of retirement. Would they receive both pay and pension? That is allowable only under certain conditions which I do not care to mention here.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I admit there is a good deal in what my hon. friend has suggested. The situation is simply this: We want to enroll this reserve" at once, as it appears desirable in certain sections of the country that they should be enrolled, and we want to make the inducements as generous as possible. The time the men would serve would not count for any additional pension. And the amount of pension the members of the force receive is very small. I beg to move that subsection (7) of section 11 be amended by substituting the word " two " for the word " one " in line 10.
Major-General MEWBURN:	After an
active officer in the Militia retires he goes on the reserve of officers, so that he can be called upon in case of emergencv. During peace time he is permitted to resign after three months' notice, I think. Our object in the Militia is to create a reserve so that the men will be available in case of emergency.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
According to the Bill
he could resign while on service.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 16:

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I beg to move that there be inserted in the Bill as section 16 the following:
Subsection (c) of section 60 of the Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
(c) to every officer in the force on the first day of July. 1902.
Section 60 created this pension system for the officers of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. Prior to that, they had certain rights to a pension under the Civil Service Superannuation and Retirement Act. When the Mounted Police Act was amended by creating a pension fund to which the officers of the force must contribute, every officer was given a certain period in which to
[Mr. Rowell. 1
elect whether he would come in under the Mounted Police Act or retain his rights under the Civil Service Superannuation and Retirement Act. There were two officers of the force out in the North country, either in the Yukon on the Mackenzie River district, I am not sure which, who were not able to take advantage of the Act in time, and they have been unable to come in under its provisions in consequence. They have wanted to do so, but as the Act was not being amended, it has not been possible to permit them to come in. The amendment I have proposed is simply to enable them to take advantage of the opportunity enabling all the officers to come in under the Act, and of which the great majority have taken advantage.

Amendment agreed to.
Bill as amended reported.
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Rowell, the House adjourned at 10.45 p.m.
Thursday, May 22, 1919.
